subtopic_detail: deciding against radiographs before reducing a radial head subluxation in a toddler
stem:
You are the doctor on the afternoon shift in a regional emergency department. A 2 year old girl is brought in by her father, who lifted her by one hand onto a kerb about an hour ago to stop her stepping onto the road. She cried immediately and has not used her left arm since.

She is fully immunised, has had no previous fractures and is otherwise well. She sits happily on her father's lap eating a biscuit with her right hand. The left arm hangs at her side with the elbow slightly flexed and the palm facing backwards. She lets you palpate the clavicle, humerus, forearm and wrist without protest, and there is no swelling, bruising or deformity anywhere along the limb. She cries only when you attempt to turn the left palm upwards.

data_table.Examination: Left arm held adducted, elbow flexed about 20 degrees, forearm pronated; no swelling, bruising, deformity or focal bone tenderness; distal pulses and capillary refill normal; skin intact

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Perform a supination and flexion manoeuvre at the elbow and reassess her use of the arm after fifteen minutes
options.rationale: Axial traction on a pronated forearm with a limb that is non-tender and free of swelling is the classic radial head subluxation, which is a clinical diagnosis treated by reduction without imaging. Supination with flexion, or hyperpronation, restores spontaneous use within minutes in most children. (Source: RCH CPG: Pulled elbow)

options.text: Apply a broad arm sling for comfort and arrange review in the paediatric fracture clinic within one week
options.rationale: A sling treats the pain but leaves the annular ligament entrapped, so the child continues not to use the arm for days. Slings belong to undisplaced fractures, where the diagnosis has already been made radiologically. (Source: RCH CPG: Pulled elbow)

options.text: Immobilise the limb in an above elbow backslab and repeat clinical assessment with radiographs in ten days
options.rationale: Backslab immobilisation with delayed imaging is the pathway for a suspected occult fracture, which requires focal bone tenderness or a fall onto the outstretched hand. Neither feature is present here. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Radial head subluxation)
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Radial head subluxation

options.text: Refer for an urgent ultrasound of the elbow to look for a joint effusion before deciding on treatment
options.rationale: Ultrasound can show a displaced annular ligament but adds cost and delay to a diagnosis already secure on history and examination. It is reserved for children whose arm use does not return after two reduction attempts. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Radial head subluxation)
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Radial head subluxation

options.text: Arrange radiographs of the elbow and forearm before attempting any manipulation of the limb
options.rationale: Radiographs are reserved for an atypical mechanism, visible swelling or deformity, or focal bone tenderness, none of which are present. Imaging a classic traction injury delays a manoeuvre that usually restores function within minutes. (Source: RCH CPG: Pulled elbow)

explanation.summary: Radial head subluxation accounts for a large share of upper limb presentations in children under five and is diagnosed on the combination of a longitudinal traction mechanism, a pronated arm held still, and the absence of swelling, bruising or focal bone tenderness. The differential that matters is a supracondylar or forearm fracture, which follows a fall rather than a pull and almost always produces swelling or point tenderness. Reduction is performed at the bedside without analgesia in most children, and a child who resumes using the arm within fifteen minutes needs no imaging and no follow up. Recurrence is common until about five years of age, so parents should be warned against lifting the child by the hands. Persistent non use after two attempts should prompt radiographs, because an occult fracture has then become the likely explanation.
key_points: The mechanism is axial traction on an extended, pronated arm, not a fall
Absence of swelling, bruising and focal bone tenderness effectively excludes fracture in this age group
Supination with flexion and hyperpronation are both acceptable reduction techniques
Return of spontaneous arm use within fifteen minutes confirms the diagnosis retrospectively
Radiographs are indicated only after failed reduction or when examination raises fracture concern
explanation.pearls: Hyperpronation reduces radial head subluxation on the first attempt slightly more often than supination and flexion and is reported by children as less painful, so it is a reasonable first technique in a distressed toddler.

sources.label: BMJ Best Practice: Radial head subluxation

subtopic_detail: first line management of a persistent infant head tilt with restricted neck rotation
stem:
You are the doctor reviewing a 9 week old boy in a community paediatric clinic. His mother says that since about three weeks of age his head has always tipped towards the right shoulder and he prefers to look to the left. She has noticed that the back of his head is becoming flatter on the right side. He was born at term by forceps delivery, feeds well and is gaining weight along the 50th centile.

On examination he holds his head tilted to the right with the chin turned to the left. You feel a firm, painless swelling within the right sternocleidomastoid. Passive rotation of the head to the right is limited to about 50 degrees, and lateral flexion to the left is similarly restricted. His eyes move together in all directions with a normal red reflex, tone and reflexes are normal in all four limbs, and both hips abduct fully and symmetrically with no clunk.

data_table.Examination: Right head tilt with left chin rotation; firm non-tender mass in right sternocleidomastoid; passive right rotation limited to 50 degrees; right occipital flattening; hips abduct fully with negative Ortolani and Barlow; neurological examination normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Request an urgent magnetic resonance scan of the cervical spine to exclude a structural or neurological cause for the tilt
options.rationale: Imaging is indicated when the tilt is of later onset, painful, or accompanied by abnormal neurology, abnormal eye movements or a fixed bony deformity, none of which apply. A normal neurological and ocular examination with a palpable muscle mass makes a structural cause very unlikely. (Source: RCH CPG: Torticollis)

options.text: Reassure his mother that infant head preference resolves spontaneously and arrange a routine review at his twelve month check
options.rationale: Positional preference with full passive range does resolve spontaneously, but this infant has a genuine restriction of passive rotation, which does not. Waiting until twelve months moves him past the window in which stretching is most effective. (Source: RCH CPG: Torticollis)

options.text: Refer him to a paediatric physiotherapist for a stretching and positioning programme and review his progress in six weeks
options.rationale: Restricted passive rotation with a palpable sternocleidomastoid mass in an otherwise normal infant is congenital muscular torticollis, and supervised stretching started before three months of age resolves the great majority without surgery. The plagiocephaly is positional and corrects as rotation is regained. (Source: RCH CPG: Torticollis)

options.text: Arrange an ultrasound of both hips before starting any treatment because of the recognised association with dysplasia
options.rationale: Hip dysplasia is associated with congenital muscular torticollis, but a clinical hip examination that is fully normal at this age is the screen, and imaging is added only if the examination is abnormal or other risk factors are present. This would delay the treatment that actually changes outcome. (Source: RCH CPG: Developmental dysplasia of the hip)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Developmental dysplasia of the hip

options.text: Fit a cranial remoulding orthosis now to correct the occipital flattening before the skull sutures begin to fuse
options.rationale: A helmet addresses the secondary skull shape and not the shortened muscle that is causing it, and it is considered only after several months of failed repositioning and physiotherapy. Treating the cause first usually makes the orthosis unnecessary. (Source: RCH CPG: Torticollis)

explanation.summary: Congenital muscular torticollis usually presents in the first two months as a head tilt towards a shortened sternocleidomastoid with the chin rotated away, often with a palpable fibrous mass within the muscle. The key examination finding is restriction of passive rotation and contralateral lateral flexion, which distinguishes it from a simple positional preference in which passive range is full. Secondary deformational plagiocephaly develops because the infant consistently rests on the same part of the skull, and it improves once rotation is restored. Outcomes depend strongly on how early physiotherapy begins, with treatment started before three months resolving the deformity in the large majority of infants. Ocular causes, cervical spine anomalies and posterior fossa lesions should be considered when the tilt is late in onset, painful, or accompanied by abnormal neurology.
key_points: Restricted passive rotation separates muscular torticollis from positional head preference
A palpable sternocleidomastoid mass is present in a substantial minority and is not a tumour
Deformational plagiocephaly is secondary and corrects as the neck restriction resolves
Physiotherapy started before three months of age gives the best resolution rates
Abnormal eye movements, pain or abnormal neurology mandate imaging rather than physiotherapy
explanation.pearls: Every infant with congenital muscular torticollis needs a careful hip examination at the same visit, because developmental dysplasia of the hip coexists in roughly one in five and both conditions share the same intrauterine crowding mechanism.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Developmental dysplasia of the hip

subtopic_detail: dietary management of chronic non-specific loose stools in a thriving preschooler
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 2 year old boy whose parents are worried about his bowels. For four months he has passed three to five loose stools a day, usually worse later in the day, and they often see recognisable pieces of carrot and corn in the nappy. He has never woken overnight to open his bowels and has never passed blood.

He drinks about 900 mL of apple juice and cordial across the day in a sippy cup and eats a low fat diet because his parents are health conscious. His weight and height have tracked steadily along the 60th centile since birth and his energy is undiminished. Abdominal examination is normal with no distension, mass or perianal abnormality. Coeliac serology with a total immunoglobulin A, a full blood count, ferritin and faecal calprotectin taken by the practice nurse last week are all within normal limits.

data_table.Growth: Weight and height both tracking the 60th centile with no centile crossing
data_table.Investigations: Tissue transglutaminase immunoglobulin A negative with normal total immunoglobulin A; full blood count, ferritin and faecal calprotectin all within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Begin a strict cow milk protein elimination diet for the whole family for four weeks and then reintroduce dairy slowly
options.rationale: Cow milk protein allergy causing loose stools presents in infancy with blood or mucus, faltering growth or atopy, and rarely begins at this age in a thriving child. Elimination diets in a two year old risk calcium and energy shortfall without addressing the osmotic load. (Source: RCH CPG: Chronic diarrhoea)

options.text: Send three faecal specimens for microscopy, culture and parasite examination and withhold treatment pending those results
options.rationale: Persistent infection such as giardiasis is worth excluding when there is weight loss, overseas travel, or a childcare outbreak, none of which are described. Four months of stable growth with a normal calprotectin argues strongly against an infective or inflammatory cause. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal)

options.text: Prescribe a course of an oral probiotic preparation and a bulking agent and arrange a further review in three months
options.rationale: Probiotics and bulking agents have at best a marginal effect on this condition and leave the driving dietary factors untouched. They also risk framing a benign functional pattern as a disease requiring medication. (Source: RCH CPG: Chronic diarrhoea)

options.text: Refer him to a paediatric gastroenterologist for upper endoscopy and colonoscopy with biopsies to establish a tissue diagnosis
options.rationale: Endoscopy is warranted for growth failure, blood in the stool, nocturnal symptoms or a raised calprotectin, and none are present. Submitting a thriving toddler to anaesthesia for a dietary problem is disproportionate. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal)

options.text: Reduce the fruit juice and cordial substantially, increase dietary fat towards normal for age, and review him in six weeks
options.rationale: Normal growth, daytime only symptoms, undigested food in the stool and a high osmotic fluid load with a low fat intake define chronic non-specific diarrhoea of childhood, which responds to correcting these four dietary factors. Reducing the sorbitol and fructose load slows transit enough for the stool to reform. (Source: RCH CPG: Chronic diarrhoea)

explanation.summary: Chronic non-specific diarrhoea of childhood, often called toddler diarrhoea, is the commonest cause of persistent loose stools between one and five years of age and is a positive diagnosis rather than one of exclusion. It is driven by a combination of excessive fluid intake, high fructose and sorbitol loads from juice and cordial, a low fat intake, and excess fibre, all of which shorten intestinal transit. The features that permit a confident diagnosis are preserved growth, absence of nocturnal stools, absence of blood, and undigested food fragments in the stool. Correcting the dietary pattern resolves symptoms within weeks in most children, and the condition remits spontaneously by school age. Failure to improve after genuine dietary change, or the emergence of growth faltering, nocturnal symptoms or blood, should trigger referral rather than a longer dietary trial.
key_points: Preserved growth and absent nocturnal stools are the two most reassuring features
Fruit juice, cordial and low fat intake are the modifiable drivers
Undigested vegetable matter in the stool reflects rapid transit, not malabsorption
Coeliac serology requires a total immunoglobulin A alongside it to be interpretable
A normal faecal calprotectin makes inflammatory bowel disease highly unlikely in this age group
explanation.pearls: Capping total juice at about 120 mL per day and lifting fat to roughly 35 to 40 per cent of energy intake will resolve most toddler diarrhoea within two to four weeks, which is why a six week review is long enough to judge the response.

subtopic_detail: separating benign nocturnal limb pains from a pain pattern that requires investigation
stem:
You are the doctor seeing a 6 year old girl brought by her mother because she wakes crying with leg pain two or three nights a week. The pain is in both calves and behind both knees, lasts about half an hour, and settles with a cuddle and rubbing. By morning she is running around normally and she has never limped or refused to walk. She has not lost weight, has had no fevers and plays a full season of netball.

Her mother is frightened because a family friend's child was recently diagnosed with leukaemia. On examination she is well grown and afebrile. There is no joint swelling, warmth or restriction, no bony tenderness over the tibiae or femora, no lymphadenopathy, no bruising and no hepatosplenomegaly. Her gait, spine and hips are normal.

data_table.Examination: No joint swelling, warmth or restricted range; no bone tenderness on direct palpation of long bones; no lymphadenopathy, bruising, pallor or hepatosplenomegaly; normal gait and hip range

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Prescribe regular evening ibuprofen for six weeks and review her response to the trial at the end of that period
options.rationale: Scheduled anti-inflammatory therapy exposes a well child to gastric and renal risk for pains that resolve within half an hour without drugs. Regular dosing also obscures the diagnostic value of any future pain pattern. (Source: RCH CPG: Growing pains)

options.text: Explain the benign pain pattern, advise simple measures at night, and arrange review if any daytime pain or limp appears
options.rationale: Bilateral pain confined to the evening and night, resolving completely by morning, with a normal examination and normal growth, is benign nocturnal limb pain, for which explanation and safety netting are the treatment. Naming the red flags that would change the plan is what makes this safe rather than dismissive. (Source: RCH CPG: Growing pains)

options.text: Order a full blood count, blood film, inflammatory markers and a lactate dehydrogenase before offering any reassurance
options.rationale: Blood tests are indicated when pain is unilateral, persists into the day, wakes the child in the second half of the night, or is accompanied by systemic features, none of which are present. Investigating a textbook benign pattern medicalises it and a normal result rarely reassures an already frightened parent. (Source: RCH CPG: Growing pains)

options.text: Arrange plain radiographs of both femora and tibiae to exclude an osteoid osteoma or an occult bone lesion
options.rationale: An osteoid osteoma causes persistent localised night pain at one site that is strikingly relieved by a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug, whereas this pain is bilateral, migratory and settles with rubbing. Bilateral symmetrical pain effectively excludes a solitary bone lesion. (Source: RACGP: Musculoskeletal pain in children)

options.text: Refer her to a paediatric rheumatologist for assessment of possible juvenile idiopathic arthritis and enthesitis related disease
options.rationale: Juvenile idiopathic arthritis requires objective joint swelling or restriction persisting at least six weeks, and morning stiffness rather than night pain is its hallmark. This child is stiffness free and examination is normal. (Source: RACGP: Musculoskeletal pain in children)

explanation.summary: Benign nocturnal limb pains affect up to a third of primary school aged children and are characterised by bilateral, deep, poorly localised pain in the calves, shins or behind the knees, occurring in the evening or first part of the night and absent by morning. The diagnosis rests on a completely normal examination and normal growth, and it is not a diagnosis of exclusion requiring blood tests. The features that should redirect the assessment are unilateral pain, pain that persists or recurs during the day, limp or refusal to weight bear, localised bone tenderness, fever, weight loss, night sweats, bruising or organomegaly. Leukaemia and bone tumours in children characteristically produce persistent, progressive, often unilateral pain with systemic features rather than a stereotyped nightly pattern that vanishes by breakfast. Naming the red flags to the family explicitly converts reassurance into a shared safety net.
key_points: Bilateral, evening or night only pain with complete resolution by morning is the defining pattern
Examination and growth must be entirely normal for the diagnosis to stand
Unilateral pain, limp, bone tenderness or systemic features mandate a full blood count and film
Morning stiffness suggests inflammatory arthritis rather than benign limb pains
Explicit safety netting is more valuable than a normal blood test for parental reassurance
explanation.pearls: Pain that reliably wakes a child in the second half of the night and is relieved within twenty minutes of ibuprofen should raise osteoid osteoma, which is the one benign bone lesion that mimics growing pains but is almost always unilateral and fixed to a single site.

subtopic_detail: making a positive diagnosis of a functional abdominal pain disorder in a school aged child
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in a general outpatient clinic reviewing an 8 year old girl referred with six months of recurrent central abdominal pain. The pain comes on most school mornings, lasts an hour or two, and is not related to meals or to opening her bowels. She has missed fourteen school days this term. She has never had pain overnight, has had no vomiting, no diarrhoea and no blood in the stool, and her weight has tracked the 45th centile throughout.

Her mother describes her as a worrier who has recently changed schools. Examination shows a soft abdomen with mild periumbilical tenderness on light palpation that disappears when she is distracted, no organomegaly, no mass and a normal perianal inspection. A full blood count, inflammatory markers, coeliac serology with a total immunoglobulin A, urine microscopy and a faecal calprotectin arranged by the referring doctor are all within normal limits.

data_table.Growth: Weight and height tracking the 45th centile with no centile crossing
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, C-reactive protein and erythrocyte sedimentation rate within normal limits; tissue transglutaminase immunoglobulin A negative with normal total immunoglobulin A; urine microscopy and faecal calprotectin within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Start a strict low fermentable carbohydrate exclusion diet supervised by a dietitian and reassess her symptoms at six weeks
options.rationale: A low fermentable oligosaccharide diet has some evidence in irritable bowel syndrome with prominent bloating and altered stools, which this child does not have. Restrictive diets in school aged children also carry a real risk of disordered eating. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal)

options.text: Repeat the inflammatory markers and calprotectin in eight weeks before committing to any explanation of the symptoms
options.rationale: Serial normal tests in a child who is growing normally and has no red flags add nothing and reinforce the family's belief that an undetected disease is present. Repeat testing is warranted only if new alarm features emerge. (Source: RCH CPG: Abdominal pain, chronic)

options.text: Refer her for an upper gastrointestinal endoscopy with duodenal biopsies to exclude an inflammatory or eosinophilic cause
options.rationale: Endoscopy is indicated for dysphagia, persistent vomiting, gastrointestinal bleeding, growth faltering or a raised calprotectin, and none are present here. A general anaesthetic for a functional disorder carries risk without diagnostic yield. (Source: RCH CPG: Abdominal pain, chronic)

options.text: Give a positive diagnosis of a functional abdominal pain disorder and arrange a school return plan with psychological support
options.rationale: Six months of periumbilical pain without alarm features, with normal growth and normal screening tests, meets the criteria for a functional abdominal pain disorder, which is diagnosed positively rather than by exhaustion of tests. Restoring school attendance and addressing the anxiety are the interventions that change the trajectory. (Source: RCH CPG: Abdominal pain, chronic)

options.text: Commence a proton pump inhibitor for eight weeks and judge the diagnosis by whether her symptoms respond to that trial
options.rationale: Acid suppression helps epigastric pain with reflux or dyspeptic features, not periumbilical pain unrelated to meals. Using a drug trial as a diagnostic test also risks attributing natural fluctuation to the medication. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal)

explanation.summary: Functional abdominal pain disorders account for the large majority of chronic abdominal pain in school aged children and are defined by symptom criteria rather than by the absence of every alternative. Alarm features that shift the assessment include involuntary weight loss or centile crossing, growth deceleration, pain that wakes the child from sleep, persistent vomiting, dysphagia, gastrointestinal blood loss, unexplained fever, arthritis, perianal disease and a family history of inflammatory bowel disease or coeliac disease. Pain that clusters around school mornings, improves at weekends and is associated with anxiety or a recent transition is characteristic, and school avoidance rapidly becomes self-reinforcing. Effective management combines an explicit positive explanation of gut and brain signalling, a graded return to school, and psychological therapies such as cognitive behavioural therapy or gut directed hypnotherapy. Continued investigation in the absence of alarm features prolongs disability and strengthens illness beliefs.
key_points: A functional disorder is diagnosed positively on symptom pattern, not by exclusion alone
Normal growth and a normal faecal calprotectin carry most of the reassurance value
Pain waking a child from sleep is an alarm feature, unlike pain on waking in the morning
School avoidance compounds disability and needs an explicit graded return plan
Cognitive behavioural therapy and gut directed hypnotherapy have the strongest evidence in children
explanation.pearls: Tenderness that vanishes when the child is distracted during palpation, sometimes elicited by re-palpating with the stethoscope, is a useful bedside sign favouring a functional disorder over an inflammatory abdominal process.

subtopic_detail: investigation priorities for a capillary malformation involving the ophthalmic trigeminal territory
stem:
You are the doctor in a paediatric clinic seeing a 7 week old girl whose parents want advice about a birthmark. A flat, sharply demarcated dark pink patch has been present since birth over the right forehead, upper eyelid and the bridge of the nose. It has not grown thicker or raised, has not ulcerated, and has not changed in size relative to her face. There are no other skin lesions.

She was born at term, feeds well and is gaining weight normally. Her parents have read about birthmarks that shrink on their own and want to know whether she needs any treatment. Neurological examination is normal with symmetrical tone and movements, and she fixes and follows. The lesion blanches incompletely with pressure and the underlying tissues feel soft and non-pulsatile.

data_table.Examination: Flat, sharply demarcated, incompletely blanching dark pink patch over the right forehead, upper eyelid and nasal bridge; no thickening, warmth, bruit or ulceration; head circumference on the 50th centile; normal tone, symmetrical movements, fixes and follows

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange brain magnetic resonance imaging with contrast and refer her for a formal ophthalmological assessment of intraocular pressure
options.rationale: A capillary malformation involving the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve carries a substantial risk of leptomeningeal angiomatosis and of ipsilateral glaucoma, so imaging and measured intraocular pressure are both required. Identifying either early allows seizure treatment and sight saving intervention before damage is established. (Source: RCH CPG: Vascular anomalies)

options.text: Reassure the parents that this mark will fade substantially over the first year and arrange review at her eighteen month immunisation visit
options.rationale: Capillary malformations persist lifelong, darken and may thicken with age, so the natural history offered here is that of a different lesion. Deferring assessment to eighteen months would also miss the window for detecting glaucoma. (Source: RCH CPG: Vascular anomalies)

options.text: Refer her directly for pulsed dye laser therapy as the first intervention and defer any further investigation until after treatment
options.rationale: Pulsed dye laser does lighten capillary malformations and is best started early, but it is a cosmetic intervention that does nothing about the neurological and ocular risks. Treating the skin before excluding those associations inverts the priorities. (Source: RCH CPG: Vascular anomalies)

options.text: Organise an electroencephalogram now and commence prophylactic levetiracetam because of the high lifetime risk of epilepsy
options.rationale: Seizures occur in most children with leptomeningeal involvement, but an electroencephalogram in an asymptomatic infant is insensitive and prophylactic anticonvulsants are not established practice. The imaging result determines whether neurology involvement is needed at all. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Sturge-Weber syndrome)

options.text: Commence oral propranolol with an escalating dose schedule and cardiovascular monitoring during the first week of therapy
options.rationale: Propranolol treats an infantile haemangioma, which is a proliferative vascular tumour that appears in the weeks after birth, grows and becomes raised, then involutes. A flat lesion present fully formed at birth that has not changed is a capillary malformation, which does not respond to propranolol. (Source: RCH CPG: Vascular anomalies)

explanation.summary: Capillary malformations, often called port wine stains, are present at birth, grow only in proportion to the child, and persist for life, in contrast to infantile haemangiomas which appear after birth, proliferate, then involute. The clinical significance of a facial capillary malformation depends on its distribution, and involvement of the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve, particularly the forehead and upper eyelid, is associated with Sturge-Weber syndrome. That syndrome comprises the cutaneous malformation with a leptomeningeal vascular malformation and ipsilateral glaucoma, and it arises from a somatic mosaic GNAQ mutation. Seizures typically begin in the first year and are associated with progressive hemiparesis and developmental impairment if uncontrolled, so early recognition matters. Glaucoma may be present at birth or develop later, which is why ophthalmological surveillance continues throughout childhood rather than being a single assessment.
key_points: A flat vascular lesion fully formed at birth is a malformation, not a haemangioma
Ophthalmic trigeminal distribution, especially forehead and upper eyelid, drives the risk
Leptomeningeal angiomatosis and ipsilateral glaucoma are the two associations to exclude
Propranolol has no role in capillary malformations
Pulsed dye laser is cosmetic and does not alter neurological or ocular risk
explanation.pearls: Early magnetic resonance imaging in an infant can be falsely reassuring because leptomeningeal enhancement may not be apparent before about one year of age, so a normal early scan in a child who later develops seizures should be repeated rather than relied upon.

subtopic_detail: choosing first line treatment for impairing motor and vocal tics in a school aged child
stem:
You are the doctor in a community paediatric clinic reviewing a 9 year old boy. For two years he has had repeated eye blinking and head jerking, and over the past eight months he has added throat clearing and a repeated grunting noise. The movements wax and wane, worsen when he is tired or anxious, and briefly disappear when he is absorbed in building models. He can suppress them for a short period at a cost of mounting inner tension.

His teacher has moved him to the back of the class and other children have started imitating the grunting, and he now asks to stay home. He has no compulsions, no ritualised checking and no intrusive thoughts. There is no exposure to stimulant medication. Neurological examination including gait, tone, power, coordination and eye movements is normal, and he is growing along the 55th centile.

data_table.Examination: Frequent eye blinking, head jerking, throat clearing and grunting observed during consultation; suppressible with subsequent rebound; neurological examination including gait, tone, power, coordination and eye movements normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line treatment?

options.text: Reassure the family that childhood tics remit spontaneously and advise that no active treatment is required at this stage
options.rationale: Watchful waiting is correct for tics that do not impair function, but this boy is being socially isolated and is now refusing school, which is the threshold for active treatment. Most tics do improve by late adolescence, which does not help him this school year. (Source: RCH CPG: Tics)

options.text: Commence a serotonin reuptake inhibitor at a low dose and titrate over four weeks with review of tic frequency thereafter
options.rationale: Serotonin reuptake inhibitors treat the obsessive compulsive symptoms that frequently accompany tic disorders but have no direct effect on tics themselves. This boy has no compulsions or intrusive thoughts, so there is no target for the drug. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Refer him for a structured behavioural therapy programme teaching competing responses and tic awareness training
options.rationale: Comprehensive behavioural intervention for tics, built on habit reversal training with a competing response, is the recommended first line treatment for impairing tics in children and has effect sizes comparable to medication without drug adverse effects. Preserved suppressibility and premonitory urge, both present here, are what make the competing response technique work. (Source: RCH CPG: Tics)

options.text: Commence low dose risperidone with baseline weight, fasting glucose and lipid measurement and regular metabolic review
options.rationale: Antipsychotics reduce tic severity but carry weight gain, metabolic and extrapyramidal burden, so they are reserved for tics that remain disabling after behavioural therapy has been tried or is unavailable. Starting here skips the treatment with the better risk to benefit ratio. (Source: RCH CPG: Tics)

options.text: Commence clonidine titrated slowly with blood pressure and heart rate monitoring at each dose increase over eight weeks
options.rationale: Clonidine is a reasonable pharmacological option, particularly when attention deficit hyperactivity disorder coexists, and has a milder adverse effect profile than antipsychotics. It nevertheless sits behind behavioural therapy in the treatment sequence for a child whose tics are suppressible and who has no comorbid attention disorder. (Source: RCH CPG: Tics)

explanation.summary: Tourette syndrome requires multiple motor tics and at least one vocal tic persisting more than a year with onset before eighteen years of age, and this boy meets those criteria. Tics characteristically wax and wane, worsen with fatigue, stress and excitement, diminish during absorbing activity, and are preceded by a premonitory urge that is relieved by performing the tic. Treatment is driven by functional impairment rather than tic count, and a child who is coping well needs education and school liaison rather than therapy. Comprehensive behavioural intervention for tics teaches awareness of the premonitory urge and a competing physical response that is incompatible with the tic, plus function based strategies for situations that worsen tics. Comorbidity is the rule rather than the exception, with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder and obsessive compulsive disorder each present in a large minority and often causing more impairment than the tics.
key_points: Multiple motor tics plus at least one vocal tic for over a year defines Tourette syndrome
Treatment threshold is functional impairment, not tic frequency
Comprehensive behavioural intervention for tics is first line where available
Antipsychotics and clonidine are second line and chosen by comorbidity and adverse effect profile
Screen actively for attention deficit hyperactivity disorder and obsessive compulsive symptoms
explanation.pearls: Stimulants prescribed for coexisting attention deficit hyperactivity disorder were long avoided in tic disorders, but controlled data show they do not worsen tics on average and treating the attention disorder often reduces overall impairment more than treating the tics.

subtopic_detail: selecting focal tone treatment for dynamic equinus in an ambulant child with spastic cerebral palsy
stem:
You are the doctor in a paediatric rehabilitation clinic reviewing a 5 year old boy with spastic diplegic cerebral palsy who walks independently but tires quickly. Over the last year he has begun walking on his toes on both sides and catches his toes on the carpet.

On examination there is increased tone in both gastrocnemius and soleus with a clear catch on fast passive dorsiflexion. With the knee extended, passive ankle dorsiflexion reaches neutral only with slow stretch, but with the knee flexed the ankle dorsiflexes to 15 degrees past neutral on both sides. Hip abduction and popliteal angles are within normal limits and there is no hip migration on his most recent pelvic radiograph. Power is preserved and there is no fixed bony deformity. He has been in twice weekly physiotherapy with ankle foot orthoses worn consistently for eight months.

data_table.Examination: Bilateral increased calf tone with catch on fast passive dorsiflexion; ankle dorsiflexion to neutral with knee extended and to 15 degrees past neutral with knee flexed; popliteal angles and hip abduction within normal limits; no fixed deformity
data_table.Investigations: Pelvic radiograph shows no hip migration; gait laboratory assessment shows equinus in stance with preserved knee extension

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Commence oral baclofen titrated upward over four weeks and reassess his walking and fatigue at the end of that period
options.rationale: Oral baclofen reduces tone across every muscle group, so in a child whose problem is confined to the calves it buys focal benefit at the cost of generalised weakness and sedation. Systemic agents are preferred when spasticity is generalised and painful rather than focal and functional. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Refer him for selective dorsal rhizotomy assessment at a tertiary centre with preoperative gait analysis and strength testing
options.rationale: Selective dorsal rhizotomy is considered for children with marked generalised lower limb spasticity, good underlying strength and no dystonia, usually after focal treatments have proved insufficient. It is a substantial irreversible neurosurgical procedure for a boy whose problem is currently confined to two muscle groups. (Source: RCH CPG: Cerebral palsy)

options.text: Apply serial below knee casts changed weekly for six weeks and then return him to his existing orthoses and therapy programme
options.rationale: Serial casting is effective against a developing contracture with restricted passive range, but this boy already achieves dorsiflexion past neutral with the knee flexed. Casting also immobilises and weakens the limb in a child whose gait problem is tone driven rather than range driven. (Source: RCH CPG: Cerebral palsy)

options.text: Refer him for bilateral gastrocnemius lengthening surgery followed by a period of postoperative casting and rehabilitation
options.rationale: Surgical lengthening is for fixed contracture, where the ankle will not reach neutral even with the knee flexed and slow stretch. Operating on a purely dynamic equinus risks overlengthening and a crouch gait that is far harder to treat than the original problem. (Source: RCH CPG: Cerebral palsy)

options.text: Inject botulinum toxin type A into both gastrocnemius muscles and continue orthoses with an intensified physiotherapy block
options.rationale: A dynamic equinus that releases with knee flexion and slow stretch, with no fixed contracture, is the exact indication for focal chemodenervation, and the resulting window of reduced tone is used for intensive stretching and gait retraining. Combining the injection with orthoses and therapy is what converts a temporary tone reduction into a lasting functional gain. (Source: RCH CPG: Cerebral palsy)

explanation.summary: Equinus gait in spastic cerebral palsy may be dynamic, driven by velocity dependent hypertonia, or fixed, driven by shortened muscle and tendon, and separating the two determines the whole treatment plan. The Silfverskiold test compares ankle dorsiflexion with the knee extended and flexed, since gastrocnemius crosses the knee while soleus does not, so a range that improves markedly with knee flexion localises the problem to gastrocnemius and indicates it is not yet a fixed contracture. Focal chemodenervation with botulinum toxin type A produces about three to four months of tone reduction, which is used as a therapeutic window for stretching, strengthening and orthotic tuning rather than as a treatment in itself. Hip surveillance with serial pelvic radiographs runs in parallel throughout childhood because migration percentage rises silently. Escalation to orthopaedic lengthening or neurosurgical procedures follows the emergence of fixed deformity or generalised spasticity that focal treatment cannot address.
key_points: The Silfverskiold test distinguishes gastrocnemius tightness from a combined fixed contracture
Dynamic tone without fixed contracture is the indication for focal chemodenervation
Botulinum toxin effect lasts about three to four months and must be paired with therapy
Oral agents treat generalised spasticity at the cost of weakness and sedation
Surgical lengthening of a dynamic equinus risks iatrogenic crouch gait
explanation.pearls: Overlengthening the triceps surae in an ambulant child with diplegia converts toe walking into a crouch gait with progressive knee flexion and patellar overload, a functional deterioration that is far more difficult to reverse than the equinus it replaced.

subtopic_detail: recognising an inflammatory myopathy from a photodistributed rash with proximal weakness in a child
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar assessing a 6 year old girl referred with three months of tiredness and a rash. Her mother says she now asks to be carried up the stairs at home and can no longer climb onto the trampoline by herself, though she runs on the flat without difficulty. Brushing her own hair has become a struggle.

On examination she has a dusky violet discolouration of both upper eyelids and thickened scaly pink plaques over the knuckles of both hands. There is dilatation and tortuosity of the capillaries at the nail folds. She rises from the floor by pushing on her thighs. Neck flexion against gravity is weak and shoulder abduction is 4 out of 5 bilaterally, while grip strength and ankle dorsiflexion are full. There is no joint swelling, no fever and no lymphadenopathy. Creatine kinase is 1850 U/L (less than 200) and the erythrocyte sedimentation rate is 34 mm/h (less than 15).

data_table.Examination: Violaceous discolouration of both upper eyelids; scaly pink plaques over metacarpophalangeal and interphalangeal joints; dilated tortuous nailfold capillaries; symmetrical proximal weakness with positive Gowers manoeuvre; distal power full; no synovitis
data_table.Investigations: Creatine kinase 1850 U/L (less than 200); erythrocyte sedimentation rate 34 mm/h (less than 15); full blood count and creatinine within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Request dystrophin gene deletion and duplication analysis and refer her to a neuromuscular clinic for ongoing management
options.rationale: Dystrophinopathy causes proximal weakness with a very high creatine kinase but affects boys almost exclusively, progresses over years rather than months, and produces no rash or nailfold capillary change. The photodistributed eruption is the finding that excludes it. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association)

options.text: Refer her urgently to paediatric rheumatology for corticosteroid and methotrexate therapy with baseline swallow and respiratory assessment
options.rationale: Heliotrope discolouration with Gottron papules, nailfold capillary change, symmetrical proximal weakness and a raised creatine kinase are diagnostic of juvenile dermatomyositis, and early combined corticosteroid and methotrexate therapy reduces calcinosis and long term disability. Swallow and respiratory muscle assessment identifies the children at immediate risk of aspiration. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association)

options.text: Prescribe a potent topical corticosteroid for the hand and eyelid rash and review her in the clinic again in six weeks
options.rationale: Treating the skin alone leaves an active systemic myositis untreated, and delay in this disease is associated with calcinosis and contractures. The rash here is a marker of a systemic vasculopathy rather than a primary dermatosis. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association)

options.text: Arrange antinuclear antibody and extractable nuclear antigen testing and withhold treatment until those serological results return
options.rationale: Myositis specific antibodies help predict phenotype and risk of calcinosis or interstitial lung disease, but the diagnosis here is clinical and treatment should not wait on serology. A negative antinuclear antibody does not exclude juvenile dermatomyositis. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Juvenile dermatomyositis)

options.text: Organise a muscle biopsy of the vastus lateralis as the necessary confirmatory test before any immunosuppression is commenced
options.rationale: Biopsy remains useful when the presentation is atypical or the rash is absent, but it is no longer required when the characteristic rash, proximal weakness, raised muscle enzymes and typical magnetic resonance appearances coexist. Insisting on it delays treatment without changing the plan. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Juvenile dermatomyositis)

explanation.summary: Juvenile dermatomyositis is the commonest inflammatory myopathy of childhood and reflects a systemic small vessel vasculopathy affecting skin, muscle and sometimes gut and lung. The cutaneous signs are highly specific: a heliotrope discolouration of the upper eyelids, Gottron papules over the extensor surfaces of the finger joints, and dilated tortuous nailfold capillaries with dropout. Weakness is symmetrical and proximal, so children struggle with stairs, hair brushing and rising from the floor while distal power remains normal. Muscle enzymes may be raised but a normal creatine kinase does not exclude the diagnosis, and magnetic resonance imaging showing muscle oedema has largely replaced biopsy in typical cases. Early aggressive treatment with corticosteroids plus methotrexate is associated with lower rates of calcinosis, contracture and long term functional loss, so referral should not wait on serology or tissue.
key_points: Heliotrope rash and Gottron papules are the specific cutaneous markers
Weakness is symmetrical and proximal with preserved distal power
A normal creatine kinase does not exclude the diagnosis
Assess swallow and respiratory muscle strength at presentation for aspiration risk
Early corticosteroid plus methotrexate reduces calcinosis and long term disability
explanation.pearls: Nailfold capillaroscopy performed at the bedside with a dermatoscope and a drop of oil will show dilated loops and avascular areas in juvenile dermatomyositis, and the density of capillary dropout correlates with disease activity well enough to guide treatment decisions.

subtopic_detail: illness planning after newborn screening detects a medium chain fatty acid oxidation defect
stem:
You are the doctor in a metabolic clinic seeing the parents of a 3 week old boy. Newborn screening flagged a raised octanoylcarnitine, and confirmatory acylcarnitine profiling and ACADM gene testing have established medium chain acyl-coenzyme A dehydrogenase deficiency. He is thriving on demand breastfeeding, is neurologically normal, and has never been unwell.

His parents have been told the condition is serious and want to know what they should actually do. They ask specifically what to do when he next gets a viral illness, since their older child vomits with every winter virus. Examination is normal with no hepatomegaly and no dysmorphism. His most recent blood glucose taken at the confirmatory visit was 4.6 mmol/L (3.5 to 5.5) and liver function tests were within normal limits.

data_table.Growth: Weight tracking the 50th centile since birth
data_table.Investigations: Acylcarnitine profile shows raised octanoylcarnitine; ACADM gene testing confirms two pathogenic variants; blood glucose 4.6 mmol/L (3.5 to 5.5); liver function tests within normal limits

lead_in: What advice about intercurrent illness is most appropriate?

options.text: Withhold all protein containing feeds during illness and provide intravenous dextrose with lipid until the illness resolves
options.rationale: Stopping protein is the emergency approach to urea cycle defects and organic acidaemias, where the toxic metabolite derives from protein catabolism. In a fatty acid oxidation defect protein is not the problem and withholding it removes energy without benefit. (Source: RCH CPG: Metabolic emergencies)

options.text: Commence daily oral carnitine supplementation and reserve hospital attendance for episodes of documented hypoglycaemia
options.rationale: Carnitine supplementation is sometimes used where the free carnitine is low, but it is adjunctive and does not prevent decompensation. Waiting for documented hypoglycaemia before presenting is unsafe, because encephalopathy and arrhythmia can develop rapidly once the glucose starts to fall. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Reassure them that the condition rarely causes problems after infancy and that standard childhood illness advice is sufficient
options.rationale: Risk is highest in the first two years but persists into adult life, with decompensations reported during gastroenteritis, surgery and prolonged fasting at any age. Standard advice to withhold feeds during vomiting is precisely what precipitates crisis in this condition. (Source: RCH CPG: Metabolic emergencies)

options.text: Give a prescribed glucose polymer drink at set intervals during illness and present to hospital if feeds are not tolerated
options.rationale: This disorder is asymptomatic while the child is fed and becomes dangerous only when fasting forces a switch to fatty acid oxidation that the child cannot complete, so an emergency regimen providing frequent carbohydrate is the entire management. Escalating to hospital when feeds are refused prevents the hypoketotic hypoglycaemia and encephalopathy that cause death. (Source: RCH CPG: Metabolic emergencies)

options.text: Restrict dietary long chain fat substantially and supplement with medium chain triglyceride oil added to each daily feed
options.rationale: Medium chain triglyceride supplementation is the treatment for long chain fatty acid oxidation defects and is exactly the wrong intervention here, since the enzyme that is missing metabolises medium chain substrates. This near pair of disorders is distinguished by chain length, and the therapies do not transfer between them. (Source: RCH CPG: Metabolic emergencies)

explanation.summary: Medium chain acyl-coenzyme A dehydrogenase deficiency is the commonest inherited fatty acid oxidation disorder and is detected by newborn screening through a raised octanoylcarnitine on the acylcarnitine profile. Affected children are entirely well when fed, because the defect only becomes relevant once hepatic glycogen is exhausted and the body must generate ketones from fatty acids. The characteristic decompensation is hypoketotic hypoglycaemia with vomiting, lethargy and encephalopathy, often precipitated by a gastrointestinal illness or a long overnight fast, and it can progress to seizures, cardiac arrhythmia and death. Management is therefore preventive and consists of avoiding prolonged fasting, a written emergency regimen of frequent glucose polymer drinks during illness, and a low threshold for intravenous dextrose in hospital when oral intake fails. Families should carry an emergency letter, because the child looks well until they suddenly do not and the diagnosis is easily missed by clinicians unfamiliar with it.
key_points: Children are asymptomatic when fed; risk arises entirely from fasting
Decompensation is hypoketotic hypoglycaemia with encephalopathy, not acidosis from protein
Medium chain triglyceride oil is contraindicated and treats a different chain length defect
The emergency regimen is frequent oral glucose polymer with escalation if feeds fail
Risk persists into adulthood around surgery, fasting and gastrointestinal illness
explanation.pearls: A child with this disorder who presents unwell and vomiting should receive intravenous glucose at about 10 per cent dextrose running at maintenance or above even if the bedside glucose is still normal, because hypoglycaemia is a late feature and waiting for it forfeits the safe window.

subtopic_detail: choosing a rehydration rate when a breastfed neonate presents with a markedly raised serum sodium
stem:
You are the doctor in a regional emergency department at 2 am. A 9 day old boy born at term is brought in by his parents because he is sleepy and has fed poorly for two days. He is exclusively breastfed and his mother's milk came in late. He has had two wet nappies in twenty four hours. His birth weight was 3400 g and he now weighs 2890 g.

He is lethargic but rousable, with doughy skin, a sunken fontanelle and dry mucous membranes. Pulse rate 178 per minute, blood pressure 62/38 mmHg, respiratory rate 52 per minute, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius. Capillary refill is 3 seconds centrally. Point of care results show sodium 168 mmol/L (135 to 145), potassium 4.6 mmol/L (3.5 to 5.5), urea 14.2 mmol/L (1.0 to 5.5), creatinine 78 micromol/L (20 to 60), glucose 3.9 mmol/L (3.5 to 5.5) and venous pH 7.31 (7.32 to 7.42).

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 178 per minute, blood pressure 62/38 mmHg, respiratory rate 52 per minute, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Lethargic but rousable; doughy skin turgor; sunken anterior fontanelle; dry mucous membranes; central capillary refill 3 seconds; 15 per cent loss from birth weight
data_table.Investigations: Sodium 168 mmol/L (135 to 145); potassium 4.6 mmol/L (3.5 to 5.5); urea 14.2 mmol/L (1.0 to 5.5); creatinine 78 micromol/L (20 to 60); glucose 3.9 mmol/L (3.5 to 5.5); venous pH 7.31 (7.32 to 7.42)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate fluid management?

options.text: Give a 10 mL/kg bolus of sodium chloride 0.9 per cent, then rehydrate over at least 48 hours aiming to lower sodium by no more than 0.5 mmol/L per hour
options.rationale: Perfusion is compromised, so a modest isotonic bolus is justified first, but the accumulated deficit in hypernatraemic dehydration must then be replaced slowly because rapid correction shifts water into brain cells that have accumulated osmolytes. A ceiling of 0.5 mmol/L per hour, or about 10 to 12 mmol/L per day, with sodium rechecked every four hours, is the rate that avoids cerebral oedema and seizures. (Source: RCH CPG: Dehydration)

options.text: Give a 20 mL/kg bolus of sodium chloride 0.9 per cent repeated to a total of 60 mL/kg, then commence maintenance fluid at standard rate
options.rationale: Escalating bolus therapy to 60 mL/kg is the paediatric septic shock sequence and delivers the entire deficit within an hour, which in hypernatraemia produces an abrupt osmotic shift into the brain. This infant has compensated perfusion rather than shock, so repeated large boluses are both unnecessary and hazardous. (Source: RCH CPG: Dehydration)

options.text: Commence rehydration with glucose 5 per cent in sodium chloride 0.225 per cent calculated to replace the whole deficit within 12 hours
options.rationale: This combines a very hypotonic fluid with rapid deficit replacement, which is the fastest route to a dangerous fall in serum sodium. The free water it delivers would lower the sodium far in excess of the safe ceiling. (Source: RCH CPG: Dehydration)

options.text: Withhold intravenous fluid and pass a nasogastric tube to deliver expressed breast milk and formula top ups over the next 24 hours
options.rationale: Enteral rehydration is preferred in mild to moderate dehydration, but this infant has lethargy, prolonged capillary refill and a sodium of 168 mmol/L, which places him beyond enteral management alone. The route is also too slow to correct a rising urea and creatinine. (Source: RCH CPG: Dehydration)

options.text: Give a bolus of sodium chloride 3 per cent at 3 mL/kg to protect against cerebral oedema and then commence maintenance fluid
options.rationale: Hypertonic saline treats symptomatic hyponatraemia or raised intracranial pressure, and giving it to a child whose sodium is already 168 mmol/L would worsen the hyperosmolar state. Cerebral oedema in hypernatraemia is a complication of correcting too fast, not of the presenting sodium. (Source: RCH CPG: Dehydration)

explanation.summary: Hypernatraemic dehydration in the neonatal period most often reflects inadequate breast milk intake in the first two weeks, and the clinical signs of dehydration are deceptively mild because water is drawn from the intracellular compartment and the circulating volume is relatively preserved. Doughy skin turgor and a preserved blood pressure alongside a large weight loss should therefore prompt an immediate electrolyte measurement rather than reassurance. Brain cells generate idiogenic osmoles within hours to defend their volume against a hypertonic plasma, and those osmoles clear only slowly, so lowering the plasma sodium quickly draws water into the brain and causes cerebral oedema and seizures. The safe approach is a small isotonic bolus only if perfusion is genuinely compromised, followed by slow deficit replacement over at least 48 hours with an isotonic or near isotonic fluid, with the sodium measured every four hours and the rate adjusted to keep the fall within about 0.5 mmol/L per hour. Feeding support, weighed feeds and lactation review are as important as the fluid prescription, since the underlying problem is a feeding one.
key_points: Clinical signs underestimate the deficit because intracellular water is lost preferentially
Correct the sodium no faster than 0.5 mmol/L per hour or about 10 to 12 mmol/L per day
Replace the deficit over at least 48 hours using isotonic or near isotonic fluid
Recheck electrolytes every four hours and adjust the infusion rate to the measured fall
Establish the feeding cause with weighed feeds and lactation support before discharge
explanation.pearls: A seizure occurring several hours into treatment of hypernatraemic dehydration is usually caused by the correction rather than the disease, and the immediate response is to slow the infusion and raise the sodium content of the fluid rather than to load an anticonvulsant.

subtopic_detail: abdominal pain during a nephrotic relapse where the diagnosis is peritoneal infection rather than oedema
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar called to the ward at midnight. A 4 year old girl admitted this morning with her third relapse of steroid sensitive nephrotic syndrome has developed abdominal pain over the last six hours. She started prednisolone twelve hours ago. The nursing staff have given paracetamol and an aperient without effect.

She is miserable and reluctant to move. Pulse rate 146 per minute, blood pressure 88/50 mmHg, respiratory rate 32 per minute, SpO2 97 per cent on room air, temperature 38.2 degrees Celsius. Her abdomen is grossly distended with shifting dullness and she guards diffusely on light palpation. Bowel sounds are present. She has periorbital and pedal oedema. Albumin is 12 g/L (35 to 50), urine protein to creatinine ratio is markedly raised, white cell count is 18.4 x10^9/L (5.0 to 15.0) with neutrophils 15.1 x10^9/L, and C-reactive protein is 96 mg/L (less than 5).

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 146 per minute, blood pressure 88/50 mmHg, respiratory rate 32 per minute, SpO2 97 per cent on room air, temperature 38.2 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Grossly distended abdomen with shifting dullness and diffuse guarding; bowel sounds present; periorbital and pedal oedema; capillary refill 2 seconds
data_table.Investigations: Albumin 12 g/L (35 to 50); white cell count 18.4 x10^9/L (5.0 to 15.0) with neutrophils 15.1 x10^9/L; C-reactive protein 96 mg/L (less than 5); urine protein to creatinine ratio markedly raised; sodium 131 mmol/L (135 to 145)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Increase the prednisolone dose and add regular ranitidine, attributing the pain to corticosteroid induced gastric irritation
options.rationale: Corticosteroid related gastric pain is epigastric, is not associated with fever or guarding, and would not produce this neutrophilia and C-reactive protein. Escalating immunosuppression in an undiagnosed sepsis is actively harmful. (Source: RCH CPG: Nephrotic syndrome)

options.text: Request an urgent surgical consultation for suspected appendicitis and keep her fasted pending an abdominal computed tomography scan
options.rationale: Appendicitis remains possible and surgical review is reasonable, but pain that is diffuse rather than migratory to the right iliac fossa, in a child with tense ascites and profound hypoalbuminaemia, points to infected ascites. Computed tomography also adds radiation without changing the immediate antibiotic decision. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Nephrotic syndrome in children)
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Nephrotic syndrome in children

options.text: Perform a diagnostic ascitic tap and commence intravenous ceftriaxone without waiting for the fluid cell count and culture
options.rationale: Fever, diffuse guarding and a neutrophilia in a child with heavy proteinuria and an albumin of 12 g/L indicate infection of the ascitic fluid, which is the commonest serious infection in nephrotic relapse and is driven by urinary loss of complement and immunoglobulin. Sampling before antibiotics preserves the microbiological diagnosis, but the antibiotic must not wait for the result. (Source: RCH CPG: Nephrotic syndrome)

options.text: Give intravenous albumin 20 per cent followed by intravenous furosemide to relieve the abdominal distension and tense ascites
options.rationale: Albumin with furosemide is the correct treatment for symptomatic tense ascites or respiratory compromise from oedema, but it treats the distension while leaving an infection untreated. Diuresing an intravascularly depleted, septic child also risks precipitating circulatory collapse and thrombosis. (Source: RCH CPG: Nephrotic syndrome)

options.text: Arrange an urgent abdominal ultrasound with Doppler to exclude renal vein thrombosis before starting any antimicrobial therapy
options.rationale: Thrombosis is a genuine hazard of nephrotic syndrome and deserves consideration, but it typically causes flank pain with haematuria and a falling urine output rather than fever with diffuse peritonism and a C-reactive protein of 96 mg/L. Deferring antibiotics for imaging in suspected peritoneal sepsis costs time that matters. (Source: RCH CPG: Nephrotic syndrome)

explanation.summary: Children in nephrotic relapse are functionally immunodeficient because they lose complement factors B and D and immunoglobulin G in the urine while ascitic fluid provides a culture medium, and this combination makes spontaneous bacterial peritonitis the signature infection of the condition. Streptococcus pneumoniae is the classical organism, with Escherichia coli and other Gram negative bacilli also common, which is why a third generation cephalosporin is the empirical choice in Australia. The presentation is easily attributed to the oedema itself, to constipation from inactivity, or to corticosteroid gastritis, and fever with diffuse guarding and a raised C-reactive protein is what separates infection from those benign explanations. A diagnostic ascitic tap showing a neutrophil count above 250 cells per microlitre confirms the diagnosis, but treatment is started immediately after sampling rather than after the result. Preventive measures include pneumococcal and annual influenza vaccination, varicella immunity checks before immunosuppression, and family education that fever during relapse requires same day assessment rather than watchful waiting.
key_points: Urinary loss of complement and immunoglobulin creates a real infection risk during relapse
Streptococcus pneumoniae is the classical organism; a third generation cephalosporin is empirical therapy
An ascitic neutrophil count above 250 cells per microlitre confirms peritoneal infection
Sample the ascites first, but never delay the antibiotic for the result
Thrombosis and appendicitis are the two differentials worth actively considering
explanation.pearls: Albumin infusion during active sepsis in nephrotic syndrome should be reserved for genuine circulatory compromise, because the oncotic pull mobilises fluid rapidly and combining it with furosemide in a hypovolaemic septic child can precipitate both hypotension and thrombosis.

sources.label: BMJ Best Practice: Nephrotic syndrome in children

subtopic_detail: insulin route and disposition when new diabetes presents with marked hyperglycaemia but no acidosis
stem:
You are the doctor in a rural emergency department 240 km from the nearest paediatric unit. A 10 year old girl is brought in by her mother with four weeks of thirst, frequent urination and 4 kg of weight loss. She has been drinking constantly and has wet the bed twice this week. She is alert, conversational and hungry, and has no abdominal pain or vomiting.

Pulse rate 92 per minute, blood pressure 108/66 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 per minute, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius. Mucous membranes are moist and capillary refill is 2 seconds. Point of care testing shows blood glucose 24.6 mmol/L, blood ketones 1.1 mmol/L (less than 0.6), venous pH 7.36 (7.32 to 7.42), bicarbonate 22 mmol/L (22 to 32), sodium 134 mmol/L (135 to 145) and potassium 4.2 mmol/L (3.5 to 5.5).

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 92 per minute, blood pressure 108/66 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 per minute, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Alert and conversational; moist mucous membranes; capillary refill 2 seconds; no Kussmaul breathing; no abdominal tenderness
data_table.Investigations: Blood glucose 24.6 mmol/L; blood ketones 1.1 mmol/L (less than 0.6); venous pH 7.36 (7.32 to 7.42); bicarbonate 22 mmol/L (22 to 32); sodium 134 mmol/L (135 to 145); potassium 4.2 mmol/L (3.5 to 5.5)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Arrange an oral glucose tolerance test and a glycated haemoglobin measurement before starting insulin to confirm the diagnosis
options.rationale: A random glucose of 24.6 mmol/L with four weeks of polyuria, polydipsia and weight loss is diagnostic, and a tolerance test in symptomatic hyperglycaemia is both unnecessary and dangerous. A glycated haemoglobin can be sent for information but must not delay insulin. (Source: RCH CPG: Diabetes mellitus)

options.text: Commence oral metformin, provide dietary advice and arrange endocrinology review within two weeks to assess her response
options.rationale: Metformin is used where type 2 diabetes is likely, which would require obesity, acanthosis nigricans or a strong family history without the rapid weight loss seen here. Weight loss with four weeks of osmotic symptoms in a ten year old indicates insulin deficiency, which metformin cannot treat. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Commence an intravenous insulin infusion at 0.1 units/kg/hour with two bag fluid therapy and hourly neurological observations
options.rationale: An insulin infusion with the two bag protocol is the pathway for ketoacidosis, defined by a pH below 7.3 or a bicarbonate below 15 mmol/L, and neither threshold is met. Infusing insulin into a child who is not acidotic and is drinking freely lowers the glucose faster than necessary and commits a rural department to a resource intensive protocol without benefit. (Source: RCH CPG: Diabetic ketoacidosis)

options.text: Give a 10 mL/kg bolus of sodium chloride 0.9 per cent and recheck the venous gas and ketones in two hours before deciding
options.rationale: A fluid bolus is for impaired perfusion, and this girl has a normal heart rate, normal blood pressure, moist membranes and a capillary refill of 2 seconds. Repeating the gas without starting insulin also delays treatment of an established diagnosis that will not improve on its own. (Source: RCH CPG: Diabetic ketoacidosis)

options.text: Start subcutaneous insulin, encourage oral fluids, and arrange same day discussion and transfer to the paediatric diabetes service
options.rationale: New type 1 diabetes without acidosis and without vomiting or dehydration is managed with subcutaneous insulin and oral fluids from the outset, and this avoids the risks of an unnecessary infusion. Same day specialist discussion secures the education, dose regimen and follow up that determine the first year of control. (Source: RCH CPG: Diabetes mellitus)

explanation.summary: Roughly a third of Australian children with new type 1 diabetes present in ketoacidosis, but the remainder present with osmotic symptoms and marked hyperglycaemia while remaining well perfused and only mildly ketotic, and the two groups need entirely different pathways. Ketoacidosis is defined by hyperglycaemia with a venous pH below 7.3 or a bicarbonate below 15 mmol/L alongside ketonaemia, and it is that biochemical threshold rather than the absolute glucose value that determines whether an insulin infusion is required. A child who is alert, tolerating oral fluids and not acidotic is treated with subcutaneous insulin, which achieves the same glycaemic control while avoiding the fluid shifts and monitoring burden of an infusion. Mild ketonaemia in the range just above the normal cut off reflects the fasting and insulin deficiency and does not by itself mandate intravenous therapy. In rural settings the decision matters practically, because an unnecessary infusion may trigger a retrieval that the child does not need while still requiring same day specialist discussion for education, dosing and follow up.
key_points: Acidosis, not glucose level, determines whether ketoacidosis treatment is required
A venous pH of 7.3 and a bicarbonate of 15 mmol/L are the operative thresholds
Well perfused, alert children tolerating fluids are treated with subcutaneous insulin
Osmotic symptoms with weight loss in a child indicate insulin deficiency, not insulin resistance
Same day specialist contact is required even when the child is not acidotic
explanation.pearls: Blood ketone measurement of beta-hydroxybutyrate is more reliable than urine ketone dipsticks in this decision, because urine testing detects acetoacetate and can read strongly positive from fasting alone or read falsely low while beta-hydroxybutyrate predominates early in decompensation.

subtopic_detail: first line management of involuntary pelvic floor contraction preventing penetration
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 26 year old woman who has been with her partner for three years and has never been able to tolerate vaginal penetration. She describes a burning, tearing sensation and an involuntary tightening whenever penetration is attempted, and the same thing happens with tampons. She is distressed and says she feels broken.

She has regular cycles, no dyspareunia at other times, no abnormal discharge and no history of sexual assault. On attempted speculum examination the introital muscles visibly contract and she withdraws, so you stop. External inspection shows normal vulval architecture with no fissuring, no atrophy, no lichenoid change and no erythema. A cotton swab applied to the vestibule produces no localised tenderness. Her most recent cervical screening test, performed on a self collected sample, was negative for oncogenic human papillomavirus.

data_table.Examination: Normal vulval architecture with no fissuring, atrophy or lichenoid change; negative cotton swab test at the vestibule; visible involuntary levator contraction on attempted speculum insertion
data_table.Investigations: Cervical screening test on self collected sample negative for oncogenic human papillomavirus

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line management?

options.text: Refer her for examination under general anaesthetic to exclude a vaginal septum or other obstructing structural anomaly
options.rationale: Structural anomalies such as a transverse septum usually present with primary amenorrhoea or cyclical obstructed menstruation, and she menstruates normally. Examination under anaesthetic also removes the conscious muscle response that is the diagnostic finding. (Source: RANZCOG: Persistent vulval pain)

options.text: Refer her to a pelvic floor physiotherapist for graded dilator therapy with relaxation and desensitisation techniques
options.rationale: A negative swab test with normal vulval skin and a visible involuntary levator contraction identifies the problem as pelvic floor overactivity rather than a vestibular or dermatological disorder, and graded dilator work with pelvic floor physiotherapy is the treatment with the strongest evidence. Psychological therapy is combined with it where distress or avoidance is prominent. (Source: RANZCOG: Persistent vulval pain)

options.text: Prescribe topical lignocaine 5 per cent ointment to be applied to the vestibule before intercourse and review her in three months
options.rationale: Topical anaesthetic is used for provoked vestibulodynia, which is defined by localised tenderness on the cotton swab test, and her swab test is negative. Anaesthetising normal tissue does nothing about the muscle contraction that is actually obstructing penetration. (Source: RANZCOG: Persistent vulval pain)

options.text: Commence a topical oestrogen cream nightly for six weeks and reassess the vaginal epithelium at the end of that course
options.rationale: Topical oestrogen treats genitourinary atrophy, which produces pallor, loss of rugae and friability in a hypo-oestrogenic woman. This woman has regular cycles and a normally oestrogenised vulva, so there is no deficiency to replace. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Sexual and reproductive health)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Sexual and reproductive health

options.text: Take vulvovaginal swabs for candida and bacterial vaginosis and treat empirically with a course of oral fluconazole while awaiting results
options.rationale: Recurrent candidiasis can cause introital pain, but it produces erythema, fissuring or discharge, none of which are present, and empirical antifungal therapy for normal appearing skin delays effective treatment. Swabs are worth taking only if the examination suggests infection. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Sexual and reproductive health)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Sexual and reproductive health

explanation.summary: Genito-pelvic pain and penetration disorder, historically called vaginismus, is characterised by involuntary contraction of the pelvic floor and perineal muscles on attempted penetration, producing pain, fear and avoidance in a self-reinforcing cycle. The examination is the diagnostic tool: normal vulval architecture, a negative cotton swab test at the vestibule and a visible or palpable levator contraction distinguish it from provoked vestibulodynia, dermatoses such as lichen sclerosus, atrophy and infection. Treatment centres on pelvic floor physiotherapy with progressive dilator use, which retrains the muscular response while gradually reducing the anticipatory fear, and psychological therapy is added where avoidance, relationship distress or trauma is prominent. Attempting a forced examination is both unhelpful and harmful, since it confirms the patient's expectation that examination is unbearable. Outcomes are good with structured therapy, and most women achieve comfortable penetration within several months.
key_points: The cotton swab test separates pelvic floor overactivity from provoked vestibulodynia
Diagnosis rests on observing involuntary levator contraction, not on investigations
Pelvic floor physiotherapy with graded dilators is first line
Psychological therapy is added for prominent fear, avoidance or relationship distress
Stop the examination when the patient withdraws rather than persisting under duress
explanation.pearls: Offer the woman control of the dilator and of the pace of every examination, because patient-controlled insertion consistently outperforms clinician-led insertion in this condition and is the single most important element of the physiotherapy protocol.
