subtopic_detail: sequencing analgesia and hormonal therapy for painful periods in an adolescent not seeking contraception
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 15 year old girl with her mother. For two years she has had cramping lower abdominal pain starting a few hours before each period and lasting two days. She misses one or two school days each cycle. She is not sexually active and does not want contraception.

Her menarche was at 12 years, cycles are regular at 29 days, and bleeding lasts five days with no flooding or clots. The pain is central and does not occur between periods. She has no dyschezia, no urinary symptoms and no pain with exercise. She has been taking paracetamol 1 g when the pain becomes severe, usually several hours after it starts, with little effect. Abdominal examination is unremarkable and she declines pelvic examination, which you do not pursue.

data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft and non-tender with no mass; secondary sexual characteristics appropriate for age; no examination of the pelvis performed
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count and ferritin within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer her to a gynaecologist for a diagnostic laparoscopy to look for peritoneal deposits and adhesive disease
options.rationale: Laparoscopy is considered when pain persists despite adequate medical therapy or when there are features suggesting endometriosis such as non-menstrual pelvic pain, dyschezia, deep dyspareunia or progressive severity. None of those apply and she has had no adequate medical trial. (Source: RANZCOG: Endometriosis)

options.text: Arrange a transvaginal ultrasound scan to assess the ovaries and the posterior compartment before commencing any treatment
options.rationale: Imaging is indicated when the history suggests a structural cause, and a transvaginal approach is inappropriate in a girl who is not sexually active and has declined pelvic examination. A textbook primary dysmenorrhoea pattern does not require imaging before treatment. (Source: RANZCOG: Dysmenorrhoea)

options.text: Increase her paracetamol to a regular four times daily dose across the whole period and add a heat pack for symptom relief
options.rationale: Paracetamol does not inhibit prostaglandin synthesis in peripheral tissue to a clinically meaningful degree, so increasing its frequency addresses neither the mechanism nor the timing problem. Heat has modest benefit but is an adjunct rather than a treatment. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Start regular naproxen beginning the day before bleeding and continuing for the first two days of each period
options.rationale: Primary dysmenorrhoea is prostaglandin mediated, so a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug started before prostaglandin release and taken regularly for the painful days outperforms paracetamol taken once pain is established. Her cyclical, ovulatory, non-progressive pattern with no non-menstrual symptoms is characteristic. (Source: RANZCOG: Dysmenorrhoea)

options.text: Start a combined oral contraceptive pill taken continuously and reassess her symptom control after three months of therapy
options.rationale: Continuous combined hormonal therapy is effective and is the usual second step, but she has declined hormonal treatment and has not yet had an adequate trial of the simpler option. Offering it after a failed anti-inflammatory trial respects her preference without abandoning the option. (Source: RANZCOG: Dysmenorrhoea)

explanation.summary: Primary dysmenorrhoea arises from endometrial prostaglandin release at menstruation causing myometrial contraction and ischaemic pain, and it characteristically begins within a year or two of menarche once cycles become ovulatory. The pain is central, starts within hours of the onset of bleeding, lasts one to three days and is absent at other times in the cycle. Features that should raise the possibility of endometriosis or another secondary cause include onset well after menarche, pain outside menstruation, progressive severity, deep dyspareunia, dyschezia, cyclical bowel or bladder symptoms, and failure to respond to adequate medical therapy. Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs work best when started before or at the very onset of symptoms and taken regularly rather than as required, and this timing point is frequently the reason an apparently failed trial was not a real one. Combined hormonal contraception used continuously is the usual next step, and persistent pain despite both warrants specialist referral rather than escalating analgesia.
key_points: Prostaglandin mediated pain responds best to anti-inflammatory therapy started before onset
Regular dosing for the painful days outperforms as-required dosing
Non-menstrual pelvic pain, dyschezia or progressive severity suggest a secondary cause
Transvaginal imaging is inappropriate when the adolescent is not sexually active
Failure of adequate medical therapy, not first presentation, is the trigger for referral
explanation.pearls: Advise starting naproxen 250 to 500 mg roughly twenty four hours before the expected bleed in a woman with predictable cycles, since prostaglandin synthesis begins before flow and pre-emptive dosing converts many apparent treatment failures into responders.

subtopic_detail: immediate response when a pregnant woman discloses partner violence at a routine visit
stem:
You are the doctor conducting a routine 28 week antenatal visit in a metropolitan clinic. When you ask the standard screening questions with the woman alone, she tells you that her partner has pushed her against a wall twice in the last month and controls the household money and her phone. She has not told anyone before. She says she does not want to leave him and does not want police involved.

She is 31 years old in her second pregnancy. Symphysis fundal height is appropriate, the foetus is active and blood pressure is within normal limits. She has an old bruise on the left upper arm. Her partner is in the waiting room and has attended every visit so far. She asks you not to write anything in her handheld pregnancy record because he reads it.

data_table.Examination: Symphysis fundal height appropriate for gestation; foetal movements present; resolving bruise on the left upper arm; no abdominal tenderness

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate response?

options.text: Acknowledge the disclosure, assess immediate safety and risk to any children, and offer a warm referral to a specialist service
options.rationale: The evidence based first response is validation, a structured assessment of immediate danger including risk to children and escalation indicators such as strangulation, threats to kill and separation plans, and a facilitated referral rather than a phone number handed over. This supports her autonomy while creating the conditions in which she may act later. (Source: RANZCOG: Family violence)

options.text: Arrange an urgent ultrasound for placental abruption and admit her to the antenatal ward for continuous cardiotocographic monitoring
options.rationale: Admission and monitoring are appropriate after direct abdominal trauma or when there is bleeding, pain, contractions or reduced movements, none of which she reports. Admitting her for surveillance she does not need removes her agency and may escalate danger at home when she returns. (Source: RANZCOG: Family violence)

options.text: Invite her partner in to discuss the relationship together so that both perspectives can be heard before any plan is made
options.rationale: Joint interviewing in suspected partner violence is contraindicated because it exposes the woman to retaliation for what she has disclosed. Couples counselling is likewise not recommended while violence is ongoing. (Source: RACGP: Abuse and violence, the white book)
source_refs: RACGP: Abuse and violence, the white book

options.text: Record the disclosure in her handheld record so that every clinician she meets is informed and can respond consistently
options.rationale: Documentation is essential, but it belongs in the confidential hospital record rather than a document the perpetrator reads. Writing it where he can see it converts a clinical note into a direct safety risk. (Source: RANZCOG: Family violence)

options.text: Explain that you must contact police because the assault occurred while she was pregnant and the foetus may have been at risk
options.rationale: Mandatory police reporting of partner violence against a competent adult is not the law in Australian jurisdictions, and overriding her wishes destroys the trust that makes future disclosure possible. Reporting obligations that do exist relate to children in the household and are handled through child protection pathways. (Source: RANZCOG: Family violence)

explanation.summary: Pregnancy is a period of elevated risk for intimate partner violence, with violence commonly beginning or escalating during pregnancy and being associated with abruption, preterm birth, low birth weight and maternal death. Routine enquiry conducted with the woman alone is standard antenatal practice in Australia, and the clinical skill lies in what happens after disclosure rather than in the asking. The first response should validate the disclosure, make clear that the violence is not her fault, assess immediate danger with attention to the high risk markers of non-fatal strangulation, threats to kill, weapons in the home, escalating frequency, controlling behaviour and imminent separation, and consider any children in the household. A warm referral, meaning a direct connection to a specialist family violence service rather than a handed over phone number, substantially increases uptake. Documentation must be detailed and contemporaneous but kept in a record the perpetrator cannot access, and the woman's own assessment of her danger is the most reliable predictor available.
key_points: Enquire only when the woman is genuinely alone, never with the partner present
Validation, risk assessment and warm referral are the three components of first response
Strangulation, threats to kill and imminent separation mark the highest risk
Document in the confidential record, not in a handheld record the perpetrator reads
Children in the household trigger separate child protection consideration
explanation.pearls: A history of non-fatal strangulation increases the risk of subsequent homicide by that partner several fold and should be asked about explicitly, since women often do not volunteer it and may describe it only as having been grabbed by the neck.

sources.label: RACGP: Abuse and violence, the white book

subtopic_detail: managing a dilated fluid filled tube before assisted reproductive treatment
stem:
You are the doctor in a fertility clinic reviewing a 33 year old woman with three years of primary infertility. She had pelvic inflammatory disease at 24 and has regular 28 day cycles with a mid luteal progesterone confirming ovulation. Her partner's semen analysis is normal on two occasions.

A hysterosalpingogram shows a dilated, non-filling right tube with no spill and a patent left tube. Transvaginal ultrasound confirms a 4 cm sausage shaped anechoic right adnexal structure with incomplete septa that is separate from the ovary and is visible on a repeat scan six weeks later. Her antimullerian hormone and antral follicle count are appropriate for her age, and the uterine cavity is normal on saline infusion sonohysterography. She and her partner have decided to proceed with in vitro fertilisation.

data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft and non-tender; no adnexal mass palpable
data_table.Investigations: Hysterosalpingogram shows dilated non-filling right tube with no spill and a patent left tube; transvaginal ultrasound shows a persistent 4 cm anechoic tubular right adnexal structure with incomplete septa separate from the ovary; antimullerian hormone and antral follicle count appropriate for age; saline infusion sonohysterography shows a normal cavity; mid luteal progesterone confirms ovulation

lead_in: What should be recommended before her embryo transfer?

options.text: Proceed directly to embryo transfer without tubal surgery, since the contralateral tube is patent and her ovarian reserve is preserved
options.rationale: Patency of the other tube is irrelevant to the problem, because the damage is caused by fluid entering the cavity from the affected side. Ovarian reserve determines how many embryos are available, not whether they implant. (Source: Cochrane: Surgical treatment for tubal disease before in vitro fertilisation)
source_refs: Cochrane: Surgical treatment for tubal disease before in vitro fertilisation

options.text: Perform hysteroscopic proximal tubal occlusion with a placed device and confirm satisfactory position on imaging before transfer
options.rationale: Hysteroscopic occlusion devices were used for this purpose but have been withdrawn in Australia, and the approach carries uncertainty about device position and later removal. Laparoscopic management is the current standard. (Source: RANZCOG: Investigation and management of infertility)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Investigation and management of infertility

options.text: Laparoscopic right salpingectomy, or proximal tubal occlusion if dense adhesions prevent safe removal of the tube
options.rationale: Fluid from a hydrosalpinx refluxes into the cavity and is embryotoxic and mechanically disruptive, roughly halving implantation and live birth rates, and removing or occluding the tube restores them to expected levels. Proximal occlusion is the accepted alternative when adhesions make salpingectomy hazardous. (Source: RANZCOG: Investigation and management of infertility)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Investigation and management of infertility

options.text: Laparoscopic salpingostomy with adhesiolysis to restore tubal patency and allow a further trial of unassisted conception
options.rationale: Reconstructive tubal surgery has a role in younger women with mild distal disease seeking natural conception, but a 4 cm hydrosalpinx has a very high reocclusion rate and leaves the embryotoxic fluid problem unresolved during in vitro fertilisation. It also carries a raised ectopic risk in a retained damaged tube. (Source: RANZCOG: Investigation and management of infertility)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Investigation and management of infertility

options.text: Ultrasound guided aspiration of the tubal fluid at the time of oocyte retrieval with a course of prophylactic doxycycline
options.rationale: Aspiration at retrieval is a pragmatic fallback when surgery is declined or unsafe, but the fluid reaccumulates within days and the benefit is much smaller than definitive tubal interruption. It is a compromise rather than the recommended option. (Source: RANZCOG: Investigation and management of infertility)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Investigation and management of infertility

explanation.summary: A hydrosalpinx is a distally occluded, fluid distended fallopian tube, usually the sequel to pelvic inflammatory disease, and it has a specific and well quantified effect on assisted reproduction. Fluid tracks retrogradely into the endometrial cavity where it impairs endometrial receptivity, exerts a direct embryotoxic effect and may mechanically flush the embryo, and the result is approximately halved implantation, clinical pregnancy and live birth rates with a higher miscarriage rate. Randomised evidence shows that laparoscopic salpingectomy before in vitro fertilisation restores outcomes towards those of women without tubal disease, and proximal tubal occlusion achieves a comparable benefit when the pelvis is too adherent for safe removal. The ultrasound appearance is characteristic, with an elongated anechoic structure containing incomplete septa and a cogwheel appearance in cross section, separate from the ovary and persisting on a repeat scan, which distinguishes it from a functional ovarian cyst. Counselling should cover the small risk to ovarian blood supply from salpingectomy and the loss of any natural conception potential through that tube.
key_points: Hydrosalpinx fluid entering the cavity halves implantation and live birth rates
Laparoscopic salpingectomy before transfer restores outcomes to expected levels
Proximal occlusion is the alternative when adhesions preclude safe salpingectomy
Aspiration at retrieval is a fallback, since fluid reaccumulates within days
Persistence on a repeat scan separates hydrosalpinx from a functional ovarian cyst
explanation.pearls: A hydrosalpinx large enough to be visible on transvaginal ultrasound, rather than one detected only on hysterosalpingogram, carries the greatest adverse effect on implantation and is the group in which surgery before transfer changes outcomes most clearly.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Investigation and management of infertility
Cochrane: Surgical treatment for tubal disease before in vitro fertilisation

subtopic_detail: hormone replacement duration and dose in a young woman with gonadal dysgenesis
stem:
You are the doctor in a young adult gynaecology clinic seeing a 19 year old woman who transferred from paediatric endocrinology last year. She has 45,X gonadal dysgenesis diagnosed at age 12 during investigation of short stature and absent breast development. She completed growth hormone therapy and pubertal induction with escalating oestradiol, and now takes oestradiol with cyclical progestogen. She has a uterus and withdrawal bleeds regularly.

She tells you she has stopped taking her tablets for the last four months because she does not like taking medication and feels perfectly well. She asks whether she really needs it since she cannot conceive naturally anyway. Her blood pressure is within normal limits, her body mass index is 26 kg/m2 and her most recent echocardiogram and aortic measurements were reported as normal.

data_table.Examination: Body mass index 26 kg/m2; secondary sexual characteristics established; uterus present on prior imaging
data_table.Investigations: Echocardiogram with aortic root measurement reported as normal; thyroid function, coeliac serology, liver function and glycated haemoglobin within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice about her hormone therapy?

options.text: She should switch to unopposed transdermal oestradiol alone, since a progestogen is only needed while pubertal development continues
options.rationale: Unopposed oestrogen in a woman with an intact uterus causes endometrial hyperplasia and carcinoma regardless of age or fertility status. The progestogen requirement is determined by the presence of the uterus, not by pubertal stage. (Source: Australian Menopause Society)

options.text: She should take a combined oral contraceptive pill instead, since it delivers the same hormones and is simpler for a young woman
options.rationale: A contraceptive pill is an acceptable alternative for some women who value the convenience, but the ethinyloestradiol dose is supraphysiological and evidence favours oestradiol based replacement for bone density and blood pressure in this group. It is a second choice rather than the recommendation. (Source: Australian Menopause Society)

options.text: She should take a bisphosphonate with calcium and vitamin D instead of hormone therapy to address the bone consequences directly
options.rationale: Bisphosphonates are not established therapy for hypogonadal bone loss in a young woman and do not address the cardiovascular, genitourinary or quality of life consequences of oestrogen deficiency. They also carry uncertain implications for a woman who may later undergo assisted reproduction. (Source: RANZCOG: Premature ovarian insufficiency)

options.text: She may stop treatment now that puberty is complete, with annual bone density scanning to detect any decline in bone mass
options.rationale: Pubertal induction and long term replacement are different indications, and stopping after induction leaves decades of oestrogen deficiency affecting bone, cardiovascular risk and quality of life. Monitoring bone density detects the damage rather than preventing it. (Source: RANZCOG: Premature ovarian insufficiency)

options.text: She should continue combined oestrogen and progestogen replacement at least until the average age of natural menopause, around 51 years
options.rationale: Hypogonadism from gonadal dysgenesis is physiological replacement rather than menopausal hormone therapy, and it is continued to the age at which ovarian function would naturally have ceased to protect bone, cardiovascular and genitourinary health. A progestogen is required throughout because she has a uterus and needs endometrial protection. (Source: RANZCOG: Premature ovarian insufficiency)

explanation.summary: Women with Turner syndrome and other causes of gonadal dysgenesis require oestrogen for pubertal induction and then lifelong physiological replacement until the average age of natural menopause, because the alternative is many decades of oestrogen deficiency at an age when bone is normally being accrued and maintained. This is replacement of an absent hormone rather than menopausal hormone therapy, so the risk and benefit framing that applies to women in their fifties does not transfer, and the risks of withholding treatment substantially outweigh those of giving it. Any woman with an intact uterus needs a progestogen alongside oestrogen for endometrial protection, whatever her age or fertility status. Adherence in young adults is a recurring problem, and transition clinics should explore the reasons rather than simply reissuing the prescription. Ongoing surveillance in Turner syndrome includes aortic imaging, blood pressure, thyroid function, coeliac serology, glucose and lipids, hearing and bone density, and pregnancy through oocyte donation requires formal cardiac assessment because of the risk of aortic dissection.
key_points: Replacement continues until about age 51, the average age of natural menopause
A progestogen is mandatory whenever the uterus is present
Oestradiol based regimens are preferred over ethinyloestradiol containing contraceptives
Stopping therapy costs bone density, cardiovascular and genitourinary health
Turner syndrome surveillance includes aortic imaging, thyroid, coeliac and metabolic screening
explanation.pearls: Pregnancy achieved through oocyte donation in Turner syndrome carries a materially raised risk of aortic dissection and death, so formal cardiac assessment with aortic root imaging is required before conception rather than during pregnancy.

subtopic_detail: antibiotic selection when postnatal collapse follows a rapidly progressive soft tissue infection
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar called to the postnatal ward. A 29 year old woman who had a normal vaginal birth 36 hours ago has become acutely unwell over the past three hours with severe lower abdominal pain, vomiting and a widespread red rash. Her three year old was sent home from childcare last week with a sore throat.

Pulse rate 136 per minute, blood pressure 82/44 mmHg, respiratory rate 30 per minute, SpO2 94 per cent on room air, temperature 39.4 degrees Celsius. She has a diffuse blanching erythematous rash over the trunk, a tender uterus and offensive lochia. Capillary refill is 4 seconds. White cell count is 2.8 x10^9/L (4.0 to 11.0) with neutrophils 2.1 x10^9/L, lactate is 5.4 mmol/L (less than 2.0), creatinine 148 micromol/L (45 to 90) and platelets 78 x10^9/L (150 to 400). Blood cultures have been taken and two litres of crystalloid are running.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 136 per minute, blood pressure 82/44 mmHg, respiratory rate 30 per minute, SpO2 94 per cent on room air, temperature 39.4 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Diffuse blanching erythematous rash over trunk; tender uterus with offensive lochia; capillary refill 4 seconds; perineum intact with no wound
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 2.8 x10^9/L (4.0 to 11.0) with neutrophils 2.1 x10^9/L; platelets 78 x10^9/L (150 to 400); lactate 5.4 mmol/L (less than 2.0); creatinine 148 micromol/L (45 to 90); blood cultures taken

lead_in: What is the most appropriate antimicrobial therapy?

options.text: Intravenous aciclovir with intravenous ceftriaxone, treating for possible disseminated viral infection alongside bacterial sepsis
options.rationale: Disseminated herpes simplex can cause postnatal collapse but characteristically produces vesicular lesions and hepatitis with transaminitis rather than a diffuse blanching erythroderma. Nothing in this presentation supports empirical antiviral therapy. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Intravenous benzylpenicillin with intravenous clindamycin, alongside vasopressor support and urgent senior surgical review
options.rationale: Rapid postnatal collapse with an erythrodermic rash, leucopenia and multiorgan dysfunction indicates invasive group A streptococcal disease with toxic shock, and clindamycin is added to penicillin because it suppresses exotoxin production and works independently of bacterial growth phase. Source control assessment is required in parallel because deep infection may need operative management. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Intravenous ampicillin with intravenous gentamicin and intravenous metronidazole as standard triple therapy for genital tract infection
options.rationale: This combination is the correct empirical regimen for uncomplicated postpartum endometritis, which develops over days with fever and uterine tenderness rather than shock within hours. It lacks the protein synthesis inhibitor needed to switch off streptococcal exotoxin production. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Intravenous vancomycin with intravenous ceftriaxone, deferring any additional agent until organism identification is available
options.rationale: This provides broad coverage but again omits an antitoxin agent, and waiting for identification loses the hours in which toxin suppression matters most. Vancomycin is reserved for suspected resistant staphylococcal infection rather than being the default. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Oral amoxicillin with clavulanic acid, with escalation to parenteral therapy if she has not improved over the next six hours
options.rationale: Oral therapy has no place in septic shock with hypoperfusion, since gut absorption is unreliable and the delay is measured against a rapidly rising mortality. A six hour observation window in this physiology is unsafe. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Invasive group A streptococcal infection remains a leading direct cause of maternal death in high income countries, and the postnatal genital tract is a common portal, often seeded from a household contact with pharyngitis or impetigo. The presentation is characteristically fulminant, with severe pain out of proportion to findings, an erythrodermic rash, gastrointestinal symptoms and progression to shock within hours of the first symptom. Leucopenia rather than leucocytosis, thrombocytopenia, acute kidney injury and a high lactate are typical of toxic shock and are easily misread as viral illness in a woman who was well the day before. Treatment combines aggressive resuscitation, a beta-lactam for bacterial killing and clindamycin or another protein synthesis inhibitor to suppress exotoxin production, since streptococci in stationary phase downregulate the penicillin binding protein targets. Intravenous immunoglobulin is considered in refractory toxic shock, surgical exploration is required when deep infection is suspected, and household contacts need assessment and public health notification.
key_points: Pain out of proportion with erythroderma and shock within hours suggests invasive group A streptococcus
Leucopenia and thrombocytopenia are typical and should not reassure
Clindamycin is added for exotoxin suppression, not for additional bacterial coverage
A household contact with sore throat is a recognised source and needs follow up
Consider intravenous immunoglobulin and surgical exploration in refractory shock
explanation.pearls: Clindamycin works in this setting because it inhibits protein synthesis regardless of bacterial growth phase, overcoming the Eagle effect in which dense stationary phase streptococci downregulate penicillin binding proteins and become relatively resistant to beta-lactams.

subtopic_detail: empirical therapy for a febrile pregnant woman with a food exposure and no localising signs
stem:
You are the doctor in an emergency department seeing a 34 year old woman at 29 weeks in her first pregnancy. She has had three days of fever, myalgia, headache and loose stools. She feels the baby moving normally and has no abdominal pain, no contractions, no fluid loss and no bleeding. She mentions eating a soft cheese and prepackaged salad platter at a family gathering five days ago, and two other guests have had a diarrhoeal illness.

Pulse rate 108 per minute, blood pressure 112/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 per minute, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 38.6 degrees Celsius, foetal heart rate 158 per minute. The uterus is soft and non-tender, the cervix is closed on speculum examination and the liquor is clear. Urinalysis shows no nitrites or leucocytes, the chest is clear on auscultation, and the throat and ears are normal. White cell count is 13.8 x10^9/L (4.0 to 11.0) and C-reactive protein is 62 mg/L (less than 5).

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 108 per minute, blood pressure 112/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 per minute, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 38.6 degrees Celsius, foetal heart rate 158 per minute
data_table.Examination: Uterus soft and non-tender; cervix closed with clear liquor on speculum; chest clear; throat and ears normal; no rash or neck stiffness
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 13.8 x10^9/L (4.0 to 11.0); C-reactive protein 62 mg/L (less than 5); urinalysis negative for nitrites and leucocytes; liver function tests within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Send stool for culture and polymerase chain reaction testing and manage her supportively pending those results
options.rationale: Stool testing is insensitive for invasive listeriosis because the organism has already entered the bloodstream by the time of presentation, and supportive management forfeits the treatment window. Waiting on stool results is the classic error in this presentation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Give a single dose of intramuscular ceftriaxone, arrange outpatient review in 24 hours and provide written advice on foetal movements
options.rationale: Outpatient management of a febrile woman at 29 weeks with a raised inflammatory response leaves an evolving bacteraemia untreated and unobserved. The agent chosen also lacks activity against the suspected organism. (Source: RANZCOG: Maternal sepsis)

options.text: Administer betamethasone for foetal lung maturation and commence nifedipine tocolysis while observing her on the antenatal ward
options.rationale: Corticosteroids and tocolysis are for threatened preterm birth, and she has a closed cervix with no contractions. Tocolysis in the setting of possible intrauterine infection is also potentially harmful. (Source: RANZCOG: Preterm labour)

options.text: Take blood cultures and commence intravenous benzylpenicillin or amoxicillin at high dose while awaiting the culture result
options.rationale: An undifferentiated febrile illness in the second or third trimester after a high risk food exposure is listeriosis until proven otherwise, and blood culture is the only reliable diagnostic test because stool culture is insensitive. High dose penicillin or amoxicillin is the definitive therapy and treating empirically before confirmation prevents foetal loss, preterm birth and neonatal sepsis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Take blood cultures and commence intravenous ceftriaxone, adding metronidazole if she develops uterine tenderness or contractions
options.rationale: Cephalosporins have no useful activity against Listeria monocytogenes, which is intrinsically resistant, so this regimen would treat many causes of maternal fever but not the one suggested by the exposure history. This gap is a recognised cause of treatment failure. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Pregnant women are roughly ten to twenty times more likely than the general population to develop invasive listeriosis because cell mediated immunity is modulated in pregnancy and the placenta is a favoured site of replication. The maternal illness is typically mild and non-specific, with fever, myalgia, headache and sometimes gastrointestinal symptoms, and there may be no localising signs at all, which is why the food history carries so much diagnostic weight. High risk foods in Australia include soft and semi-soft cheeses, prepackaged salads, cold cooked chicken, deli meats, pate, raw seafood and unpasteurised dairy. Blood culture is the diagnostic test of choice, and stool culture is unhelpful because it is insensitive and the organism is carried asymptomatically. Listeria monocytogenes is intrinsically resistant to all cephalosporins, so any empirical regimen that relies on ceftriaxone will miss it, and treatment is high dose penicillin or amoxicillin, often with gentamicin in severe disease, with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole reserved for penicillin allergy outside the first trimester.
key_points: An undifferentiated fever in pregnancy with a food exposure is listeriosis until excluded
Blood culture is the diagnostic test; stool culture is insensitive and misleading
Listeria is intrinsically resistant to every cephalosporin including ceftriaxone
High dose penicillin or amoxicillin is definitive therapy, given before confirmation
Untreated maternal infection causes foetal loss, preterm birth and neonatal sepsis
explanation.pearls: Whenever a pregnant woman is given empirical ceftriaxone for an undifferentiated fever, amoxicillin must be added if listeriosis is plausible, because the cephalosporin gap in Listeria cover is the single most frequently missed point in this presentation.

subtopic_detail: definitive treatment choice after hormonal therapy fails in diffuse uterine wall disease
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar reviewing a 44 year old woman in clinic. For four years she has had progressively heavier and more painful periods with a dragging pelvic ache that persists between cycles. She has three children, has completed her family, and her partner had a vasectomy six years ago.

A levonorgestrel intrauterine system inserted twenty months ago reduced her bleeding for a time but she now bleeds heavily for eight days each month and the device remains correctly positioned on ultrasound. Tranexamic acid and continuous norethisterone have both failed. Transvaginal ultrasound shows a globular uterus with asymmetrical myometrial thickening, subendometrial linear striations and myometrial cysts, with no discrete fibroid and a normal endometrial thickness. Her haemoglobin is 98 g/L (115 to 155) with a ferritin of 8 micrograms/L (30 to 200), and an endometrial biopsy shows benign secretory endometrium.

data_table.Examination: Bulky, globular, mildly tender uterus approximately 12 weeks size; no adnexal mass
data_table.Investigations: Transvaginal ultrasound shows globular uterus with asymmetrical myometrial thickening, subendometrial linear striations and myometrial cysts, no discrete fibroid, normal endometrial thickness; intrauterine device correctly sited; haemoglobin 98 g/L (115 to 155); ferritin 8 micrograms/L (30 to 200); endometrial biopsy shows benign secretory endometrium

lead_in: What is the most appropriate definitive management to offer?

options.text: Total hysterectomy with conservation of the ovaries, together with iron replacement before surgery
options.rationale: Diffuse adenomyosis that has failed an appropriately sited intrauterine system plus two other medical agents in a woman who has completed her family is best treated by removing the diseased myometrium, which is the only intervention that reliably cures both the bleeding and the pain. Ovarian conservation at 44 preserves endogenous hormone production and avoids surgical menopause. (Source: RANZCOG: Heavy menstrual bleeding)

options.text: Endometrial ablation using a second generation device, with a repeat ultrasound scan six months after the procedure
options.rationale: Ablation destroys the endometrium but cannot reach adenomyotic tissue within the myometrium, so failure rates and reintervention are high in this condition and it does not treat the pain. It performs best when the cavity is normal and bleeding is the only symptom. (Source: RANZCOG: Heavy menstrual bleeding)

options.text: Uterine artery embolisation performed by an interventional radiologist, with clinical review three months after the procedure
options.rationale: Embolisation gives worthwhile short term symptom relief in adenomyosis but has substantially higher recurrence and reintervention rates than it does for fibroids. It is a reasonable option for a woman who declines or cannot have surgery rather than the recommended definitive treatment. (Source: RANZCOG: Heavy menstrual bleeding)

options.text: Replace the intrauterine system with a new device and add a six month course of a gonadotrophin releasing hormone agonist
options.rationale: The existing device is correctly positioned and is simply not controlling the disease, so exchanging it addresses nothing. Gonadotrophin releasing hormone agonists shrink adenomyosis but symptoms return within months of stopping and prolonged use has bone consequences. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Perform a hysteroscopic resection of the affected myometrium with concurrent adhesion prevention and follow up hysteroscopy
options.rationale: Hysteroscopic resection reaches only the cavity and immediately subendometrial tissue, which cannot address disease distributed diffusely through the wall. Deep resection also risks perforation and intrauterine adhesions. (Source: RANZCOG: Heavy menstrual bleeding)

explanation.summary: Adenomyosis is the presence of endometrial glands and stroma within the myometrium with surrounding smooth muscle hypertrophy, and it typically presents in the fourth and fifth decades with heavy menstrual bleeding, progressive dysmenorrhoea and chronic pelvic pressure. Transvaginal ultrasound has largely replaced histology for diagnosis, with a globular asymmetrically thickened uterus, myometrial cysts, subendometrial echogenic linear striations, fan shaped shadowing and an indistinct junctional zone forming the recognised criteria. Medical management is tried first, with the levonorgestrel intrauterine system having the best evidence, supported by tranexamic acid, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and continuous progestogens or combined hormonal therapy. When medical therapy fails in a woman who has completed her family, hysterectomy is the only definitive cure because the disease is within the myometrium itself, and uterine conserving procedures designed for fibroids or for endometrial pathology perform poorly. Iron deficiency should be corrected before surgery, since it is both a consequence of the disease and an independent predictor of transfusion and poor recovery.
key_points: Ultrasound criteria include a globular uterus, myometrial cysts and subendometrial striations
The levonorgestrel intrauterine system has the best medical evidence and is tried first
Endometrial ablation fails in adenomyosis because the disease is within the myometrium
Embolisation has higher recurrence in adenomyosis than in fibroids
Correct iron deficiency before surgery to reduce transfusion and improve recovery
explanation.pearls: Ferritin below about 30 micrograms per litre confirms iron deficiency even when the haemoglobin is only mildly reduced, and intravenous iron given four to six weeks before hysterectomy for heavy bleeding measurably reduces perioperative transfusion.

subtopic_detail: triage of a complex adnexal mass after menopause using a combined risk assessment
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 63 year old woman who has had six weeks of abdominal bloating, early satiety and a change in her waistband size. Her last menstrual period was at 51 years and she has had no postmenopausal bleeding. She has never used hormone therapy and has no family history of breast or ovarian cancer.

Transvaginal and transabdominal ultrasound show a 7 cm right adnexal mass with multiple solid papillary projections, internal septations thicker than 3 mm and marked colour Doppler flow within the solid components, together with a small volume of free fluid in the pouch of Douglas. Her CA125 is 310 kU/L (less than 35). A full blood count, liver function tests and renal function are within normal limits, and a recent faecal occult blood test was negative.

data_table.Examination: Abdomen mildly distended with a palpable pelvic mass; no ascitic shifting dullness clinically detectable; no palpable supraclavicular nodes
data_table.Investigations: Ultrasound shows a 7 cm right adnexal mass with solid papillary projections, septations thicker than 3 mm, marked internal colour Doppler flow and free fluid in the pouch of Douglas; CA125 310 kU/L (less than 35); full blood count, liver and renal function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer her to the general gynaecology list for a laparoscopic ovarian cystectomy with frozen section available intraoperatively
options.rationale: Cystectomy in a likely malignancy breaches the capsule and converts potentially stage one disease into stage one C, and a general list lacks the staging expertise and debulking capability required. Referral pathway, not just the operation, affects survival in this disease. (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Ovarian cancer)

options.text: Request germline BRCA1 and BRCA2 testing and defer the referral decision until the genetic result becomes available
options.rationale: Genetic testing is offered to all women with high grade serous ovarian cancer and influences treatment with targeted agents, but it follows diagnosis rather than preceding referral. Waiting weeks for a result that does not change the immediate plan is harmful. (Source: eviQ: Ovarian cancer genetic testing)

options.text: Refer her directly to a gynaecological oncology service for staging computed tomography and multidisciplinary surgical planning
options.rationale: A postmenopausal woman with a morphologically complex mass and a markedly raised CA125 generates a high risk of malignancy index, and outcomes in ovarian cancer are measurably better when the primary surgery is performed by a subspecialist within a multidisciplinary service. Staging imaging is arranged as part of that referral rather than before it. (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Ovarian cancer)

options.text: Repeat the CA125 and the ultrasound in twelve weeks to establish whether the mass and the marker are changing over time
options.rationale: Interval surveillance is appropriate for a simple unilocular cyst with a normal marker, where the risk of malignancy is very low. Delaying a high risk complex mass by three months allows disease progression and worsens the prognosis. (Source: RANZCOG: Management of ovarian masses)

options.text: Arrange an ultrasound guided percutaneous biopsy of the solid component to establish a tissue diagnosis before any referral
options.rationale: Percutaneous biopsy of an apparently operable ovarian mass risks tumour spill and upstaging, and is reserved for advanced unresectable disease where neoadjuvant chemotherapy is planned. The diagnostic and staging procedure is surgery performed by the oncology team. (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Ovarian cancer)

explanation.summary: Ovarian cancer presents with vague abdominal symptoms such as bloating, early satiety, urinary urgency and increasing abdominal size that are easily attributed to functional gut disorders, and the combination of persistent new symptoms in a woman over fifty warrants pelvic imaging and a CA125. Risk stratification in Australian practice commonly uses the risk of malignancy index, which multiplies the CA125 value by an ultrasound morphology score and a menopausal status score, with a threshold of around 200 prompting referral to gynaecological oncology. The ultrasound features carrying most weight are solid areas, papillary projections, thick septations, bilaterality, ascites and marked internal vascularity. CA125 is raised in many benign conditions in premenopausal women, including endometriosis, fibroids and pelvic inflammatory disease, which is why the marker is interpreted alongside menopausal status rather than alone. Referral to a subspecialist service before any surgery is the single modifiable factor most consistently associated with improved survival, because complete cytoreduction at the first operation is the strongest prognostic determinant.
key_points: Persistent bloating, early satiety and abdominal distension in older women require imaging and CA125
The risk of malignancy index combines the marker, ultrasound morphology and menopausal status
Solid areas, thick septations, ascites and internal vascularity are the key ultrasound features
Percutaneous biopsy risks spill and is reserved for unresectable disease
Primary surgery by a gynaecological oncologist improves survival
explanation.pearls: Complete macroscopic cytoreduction at primary surgery, meaning no visible residual disease rather than merely optimal debulking, is the strongest modifiable prognostic factor in advanced ovarian cancer and is achieved far more often in specialist centres.

subtopic_detail: acting on a non-invasive prenatal screen that fails twice for insufficient placental deoxyribonucleic acid
stem:
You are the doctor in an antenatal clinic reviewing a 38 year old woman in her second pregnancy. She chose non-invasive prenatal screening at 10 weeks. The laboratory reported no result because of insufficient placental deoxyribonucleic acid, and a repeat sample at 13 weeks has again returned no result for the same reason.

Her body mass index is 41 kg/m2 and she takes enoxaparin for a previous unprovoked venous thromboembolism. She has declined the first trimester combined screen because she wanted the newer test. An ultrasound at 13 weeks showed a single viable foetus with a crown rump length consistent with dates, a nuchal translucency of 1.4 mm and no structural abnormality seen. She is now 14 weeks and asks whether she should simply try the blood test a third time.

data_table.Examination: Body mass index 41 kg/m2; uterus palpable just above the symphysis pubis
data_table.Investigations: Non-invasive prenatal screening at 10 and 13 weeks both reported as no result for insufficient foetal fraction; ultrasound at 13 weeks shows single viable foetus, crown rump length consistent with dates, nuchal translucency 1.4 mm, no structural abnormality identified

lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice?

options.text: Reassure her that a nuchal translucency of 1.4 mm with normal anatomy provides adequate screening and that no further testing is needed
options.rationale: A normal nuchal translucency alone, without the biochemical components of the combined screen, has a detection rate for trisomy 21 of only around 70 per cent and does not address the risk signalled by the failed samples. Nuchal measurement is one component of a screen, not a screen in itself. (Source: RANZCOG: Prenatal screening and diagnostic testing)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Prenatal screening and diagnostic testing

options.text: Arrange a second trimester maternal serum quadruple test and base any decision about diagnostic testing on that risk figure
options.rationale: The quadruple test is a legitimate option for women presenting too late for first trimester screening, but its detection rate is materially lower than either the combined screen or cell free deoxyribonucleic acid testing. Offering another screening test to a woman already flagged as higher risk simply defers the decision. (Source: RANZCOG: Prenatal screening and diagnostic testing)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Prenatal screening and diagnostic testing

options.text: Arrange transabdominal chorionic villus sampling this week so that a result is available before the second trimester anatomy scan
options.rationale: Chorionic villus sampling is the correct diagnostic route between 11 and 14 weeks, but at 14 weeks amniocentesis from 15 weeks is imminent and carries a lower rate of confined placental mosaicism and of ambiguous results. Her enoxaparin also requires timing around any invasive procedure. (Source: RANZCOG: Prenatal screening and diagnostic testing)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Prenatal screening and diagnostic testing

options.text: Repeat the non-invasive screen a third time at 16 weeks, since the placental contribution rises steadily with advancing gestation
options.rationale: The fraction does rise with gestation, but a high maternal body mass index dilutes it in a larger plasma volume and two consecutive failures predict a third. Repeating a test that has already failed twice consumes weeks and leaves her without a result at a gestation where options narrow. (Source: RANZCOG: Prenatal screening and diagnostic testing)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Prenatal screening and diagnostic testing

options.text: Counsel her that repeated failure is itself associated with aneuploidy and offer diagnostic amniocentesis as well as second trimester ultrasound
options.rationale: A persistently low placental fraction is independently associated with triploidy and with trisomies 13 and 18, so two failed attempts convey risk information rather than merely a technical problem, and this is the point candidates most often miss. Amniocentesis from 15 weeks gives a definitive karyotype and microarray while the detailed anatomy scan screens for structural markers. (Source: RANZCOG: Prenatal screening and diagnostic testing)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Prenatal screening and diagnostic testing

explanation.summary: Cell free deoxyribonucleic acid screening analyses placental fragments circulating in maternal plasma, and a reliable result requires the placental contribution to reach a threshold of roughly four per cent of total cell free deoxyribonucleic acid. Failure to reach that threshold is reported as a no result and occurs in a few per cent of samples, most often because of early gestation, high maternal weight diluting the fragments in an expanded plasma volume, certain anticoagulants and technical factors. The clinically important point is that a low fraction is not merely a laboratory inconvenience: it is independently associated with triploidy, trisomy 18 and trisomy 13, all of which are accompanied by small or abnormal placentas, so women with repeated failures carry a higher aneuploidy risk than the background population. The recommended response after a second failure is therefore genetic counselling, detailed ultrasound assessment and the offer of a diagnostic test rather than a further repeat. Women should be told before testing that a no result is possible and what the pathway will be, because discovering this at 14 weeks under time pressure is far harder.
key_points: A result requires the placental fraction to reach roughly four per cent of cell free deoxyribonucleic acid
High maternal body mass index is the commonest reason for persistent failure
Repeated low fraction is independently associated with triploidy and trisomies 13 and 18
After a second failure, offer counselling, detailed ultrasound and diagnostic testing
Nuchal translucency without biochemistry is not an adequate standalone screen
explanation.pearls: Counsel women with a body mass index above about 35 before they choose cell free deoxyribonucleic acid screening that the no result rate rises steeply with weight, and that the combined first trimester screen may give them a usable risk figure where the newer test will not.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Prenatal screening and diagnostic testing
Human Genetics Society of Australasia: Prenatal screening

subtopic_detail: recognising decompensated thyrotoxicosis during labour and choosing the sequence of drug therapy
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar on the birth suite. A 27 year old woman at 39 weeks in her first pregnancy has been labouring for eight hours. She has Graves disease diagnosed in her teens and admits she stopped her propylthiouracil in the second trimester because she felt well. She has become agitated, confused and vomiting over the last hour.

Pulse rate 168 per minute in atrial fibrillation, blood pressure 96/48 mmHg, respiratory rate 32 per minute, SpO2 95 per cent on room air, temperature 39.6 degrees Celsius, foetal heart rate 190 per minute with reduced variability. She has a smooth goitre with a bruit and a fine tremor. The liquor is clear, the cervix is 6 cm dilated and there is no uterine tenderness. Point of care testing shows a white cell count within normal limits, lactate 3.2 mmol/L (less than 2.0), and a free thyroxine markedly raised with a suppressed thyroid stimulating hormone on urgent assay.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 168 per minute in atrial fibrillation, blood pressure 96/48 mmHg, respiratory rate 32 per minute, SpO2 95 per cent on room air, temperature 39.6 degrees Celsius, foetal heart rate 190 per minute with reduced variability
data_table.Examination: Agitated and disorientated; smooth goitre with audible bruit; fine tremor; warm peripheries; clear liquor; cervix 6 cm dilated; uterus non-tender
data_table.Investigations: White cell count within normal limits; lactate 3.2 mmol/L (less than 2.0); free thyroxine markedly raised with suppressed thyroid stimulating hormone; blood cultures taken

lead_in: What is the most appropriate pharmacological sequence?

options.text: Proceed to immediate category one caesarean section under general anaesthesia and commence antithyroid therapy after delivery
options.rationale: Delivery does not resolve thyroid storm and surgery with general anaesthesia in an untreated storm carries very high maternal mortality. Medical stabilisation comes first, with the mode and timing of birth decided once the maternal condition and foetal status have been reassessed. (Source: RANZCOG: Thyroid disease in pregnancy)

options.text: Give intravenous propranolol and oral propylthiouracil first, then iodine at least one hour later, with hydrocortisone and cooling
options.rationale: Beta blockade controls the adrenergic storm while the thionamide blocks new hormone synthesis, and iodine must follow the thionamide by about an hour because giving it first supplies substrate that the unblocked gland will organify into more hormone. Hydrocortisone blocks peripheral conversion of thyroxine and covers relative adrenal insufficiency. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Give oral potassium iodide immediately, then commence propylthiouracil and propranolol once the iodine has been absorbed
options.rationale: This inverts the critical sequence. Iodine given before the synthetic pathway is blocked is taken up and organified, transiently increasing hormone output in a patient who is already in crisis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Give intravenous amiodarone to control the atrial fibrillation, then commence carbimazole and hydrocortisone once the rate is controlled
options.rationale: Amiodarone carries a very high iodine load and precipitates or worsens thyrotoxicosis, so it is the wrong antiarrhythmic in this setting, and it also crosses the placenta and causes foetal thyroid dysfunction. Rate control here comes from beta blockade and from treating the underlying thyroid state. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Give intravenous broad spectrum antibiotics and paracetamol for presumed chorioamnionitis and reassess after the fever has settled
options.rationale: Sepsis must be considered and cultures taken, but clear liquor, a non-tender uterus, a normal white cell count, atrial fibrillation, a goitre with a bruit and a suppressed thyroid stimulating hormone all point to thyroid storm. Treating only for infection leaves the actual crisis untreated during its most lethal hours. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

explanation.summary: Thyroid storm is decompensated thyrotoxicosis with fever, tachyarrhythmia, altered mental state, gastrointestinal upset and cardiovascular instability, and labour, infection, surgery and abrupt cessation of antithyroid therapy are classical precipitants. In pregnancy it is readily mistaken for chorioamnionitis or maternal sepsis, and the features that discriminate are atrial fibrillation, a goitre with a bruit, a fine tremor, warm peripheries and a suppressed thyroid stimulating hormone with clear liquor and a non-tender uterus. Treatment is simultaneous on four fronts: beta blockade to control the adrenergic response, a thionamide to block new hormone synthesis, iodine given at least an hour after the thionamide to inhibit hormone release, and corticosteroid to reduce peripheral conversion of thyroxine to triiodothyronine and to cover relative adrenal insufficiency, alongside active cooling, fluids and treatment of the precipitant. Propylthiouracil is often preferred acutely because it also inhibits peripheral conversion, although carbimazole is standard for maintenance outside the first trimester. Foetal tachycardia usually reflects the maternal state and improves with maternal treatment, so decisions about birth follow stabilisation rather than preceding it.
key_points: Atrial fibrillation with fever and a goitre with a bruit separates storm from sepsis
The order matters: thionamide before iodine, separated by at least one hour
Corticosteroid reduces peripheral thyroxine conversion and covers adrenal insufficiency
Amiodarone is contraindicated because of its iodine load and placental transfer
Stabilise the mother medically before deciding on the mode and timing of birth
explanation.pearls: Propylthiouracil is preferred over carbimazole during a storm because it additionally blocks peripheral deiodination of thyroxine to the more active triiodothyronine, an effect carbimazole does not share, despite propylthiouracil carrying the greater risk of hepatotoxicity in ongoing use.

subtopic_detail: observation period and immunoglobulin dosing after blunt abdominal injury in the third trimester
stem:
You are the doctor in an emergency department receiving a 25 year old woman at 31 weeks in her first pregnancy. She was the restrained driver in a side impact collision at moderate speed forty minutes ago. She walked from the vehicle and denies loss of consciousness.

Pulse rate 96 per minute, blood pressure 118/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 per minute, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius, foetal heart rate 142 per minute. There is a seatbelt bruise across the lower abdomen. The uterus is soft between infrequent tightenings, there is no vaginal bleeding or fluid loss, and the primary survey is otherwise unremarkable. Her blood group is O RhD negative with a negative antibody screen at booking. Initial cardiotocography over thirty minutes shows a normal baseline with good variability, accelerations present, and three irregular tightenings.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 96 per minute, blood pressure 118/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 per minute, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius, foetal heart rate 142 per minute
data_table.Examination: Seatbelt bruising across lower abdomen; uterus soft between tightenings; no vaginal bleeding or liquor; primary survey otherwise unremarkable
data_table.Investigations: Blood group O RhD negative with negative antibody screen at booking; full blood count and coagulation profile within normal limits; cardiotocography over thirty minutes shows normal baseline, good variability, accelerations present and three irregular tightenings

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Send a Kleihauer test and give anti-D only if foetal red cells are detected in the maternal circulation on that assay
options.rationale: Anti-D is indicated for every RhD negative woman after a potentially sensitising event regardless of the Kleihauer result, because the assay is insensitive to very small bleeds that can still sensitise. Making the decision to treat contingent on the test inverts its purpose, which is to quantify a large bleed and add further doses. (Source: Australian Red Cross Lifeblood: Anti-D guidelines)
source_refs: Australian Red Cross Lifeblood: Anti-D guidelines

options.text: Administer betamethasone and commence nifedipine tocolysis to suppress the uterine activity, and admit her for overnight observation
options.rationale: Tocolysis after abdominal trauma is potentially dangerous because suppressing contractions removes the earliest and most sensitive sign of an evolving abruption. Corticosteroids are given if preterm birth becomes likely, which is a decision made during rather than before the observation period. (Source: RANZCOG: Trauma in pregnancy)

options.text: Discharge her now with written advice about bleeding, pain and foetal movements, and review her at her next scheduled visit
options.rationale: A reassuring thirty minute trace does not exclude abruption, which characteristically declares itself over the following hours through increasing uterine activity rather than at presentation. Discharge at this point misses the window in which deterioration is detected. (Source: RANZCOG: Trauma in pregnancy)

options.text: Continue cardiotocography for at least four hours, send a Kleihauer test and give anti-D with any additional dose guided by that result
options.rationale: A minimum of four hours of continuous monitoring is required after significant blunt abdominal trauma because abruption is heralded by frequent uterine activity that emerges over hours, and persistent contractions extend monitoring to twenty four hours. The Kleihauer here serves to quantify the bleed and calculate additional anti-D beyond the standard dose, not to decide whether to give it. (Source: RANZCOG: Trauma in pregnancy)

options.text: Arrange an urgent ultrasound scan to exclude retroplacental clot and discharge her if the placenta appears sonographically normal
options.rationale: Ultrasound has poor sensitivity for acute abruption because fresh blood is isoechoic with placenta, so a normal scan carries little reassurance. Cardiotocography detects abruption far more reliably than imaging in this setting. (Source: RANZCOG: Trauma in pregnancy)

explanation.summary: Trauma complicates a few per cent of pregnancies and is a leading non-obstetric cause of maternal and foetal death, with motor vehicle collisions the commonest mechanism. Placental abruption is the injury that matters most, because the elastic myometrium deforms while the relatively inelastic placenta does not, shearing the two apart, and it can occur after apparently minor impacts and with no external bleeding. Cardiotocography is the most sensitive detector of abruption after trauma, and the relevant signal is uterine activity: fewer than about one contraction in ten minutes over four hours is reassuring, whereas more frequent activity extends monitoring to twenty four hours. Ultrasound is poorly sensitive for acute abruption because fresh retroplacental blood has similar echogenicity to placenta, so a normal scan should never end the observation period. Every RhD negative woman receives anti-D after a potentially sensitising event, with the Kleihauer or flow cytometry used to quantify the feto-maternal haemorrhage and calculate additional doses beyond the standard amount rather than to decide whether to treat at all.
key_points: Abruption after trauma may occur without external bleeding and after minor impacts
Minimum four hours of continuous cardiotocography; extend to 24 hours if contractions persist
Uterine activity frequency is the key signal, more sensitive than ultrasound
Give anti-D to every RhD negative woman regardless of the Kleihauer result
Avoid tocolysis, which masks the earliest sign of an evolving abruption
explanation.pearls: Counsel every pregnant woman to keep wearing a three point seatbelt with the lap portion low across the hips beneath the uterus and the sash between the breasts, because correctly worn restraints reduce foetal loss substantially whereas an unrestrained or incorrectly placed belt increases uterine injury.

sources.label: Australian Red Cross Lifeblood: Anti-D guidelines

subtopic_detail: anticoagulation choice in early pregnancy for a woman with a prosthetic heart valve
stem:
You are the doctor in a combined obstetric medicine clinic seeing a 30 year old woman who is 6 weeks pregnant with her first child. She has a mechanical bileaflet mitral valve replaced at 24 years for rheumatic disease and takes warfarin 4 mg daily with a stable international normalised ratio between 2.5 and 3.5. She did not plan the pregnancy and only stopped her contraception two months ago.

She is well, with no breathlessness, no orthopnoea and no palpitations. Examination reveals crisp prosthetic sounds with no murmur of regurgitation, clear lung fields and no peripheral oedema. Her most recent transthoracic echocardiogram six months ago showed normal prosthetic gradients and normal left ventricular function. She is frightened by what she has read about warfarin and wants to know what she should take for the rest of the pregnancy.

data_table.Examination: Crisp prosthetic valve sounds with no regurgitant murmur; chest clear; no peripheral oedema; jugular venous pressure not elevated
data_table.Investigations: International normalised ratio stable between 2.5 and 3.5 on warfarin 4 mg daily; transthoracic echocardiogram six months ago shows normal prosthetic gradients and normal left ventricular systolic function; full blood count and renal function within normal limits

lead_in: What anticoagulation strategy should you recommend for the remainder of the first trimester?

options.text: Continue warfarin at her current daily dose, since it remains below the threshold at which embryopathy risk rises appreciably
options.rationale: Warfarin gives the lowest maternal valve thrombosis risk, and embryopathy risk is dose dependent, being low at daily doses at or below about 5 mg and rising substantially above that. Continuing a low dose through organogenesis is the recommended strategy when the required dose is small, provided she is fully informed of the residual foetal risk. (Source: RANZCOG: Cardiac disease in pregnancy)

options.text: Stop the warfarin and use prophylactic dose enoxaparin once daily throughout pregnancy with monthly anti-factor Xa monitoring
options.rationale: Prophylactic dosing is grossly inadequate for a mechanical valve and would expose her to a high risk of valve thrombosis, which carries substantial maternal mortality. If heparin is used, it must be therapeutic, twice daily and dose adjusted to peak anti-factor Xa levels. (Source: RANZCOG: Cardiac disease in pregnancy)

options.text: Stop all anticoagulation until 12 weeks and add low dose aspirin, restarting warfarin once organogenesis has been completed
options.rationale: Any period without anticoagulation in a mechanical valve risks valve thrombosis, which is rapidly fatal, and aspirin provides no meaningful protection against it. The pregnancy itself is prothrombotic, which compounds the hazard. (Source: RANZCOG: Cardiac disease in pregnancy)

options.text: Stop the warfarin and commence unfractionated heparin by continuous infusion as an inpatient for the whole first trimester
options.rationale: Continuous unfractionated heparin is an accepted option for a woman who chooses to avoid all warfarin exposure, but it requires prolonged admission and carries higher rates of valve thrombosis and of heparin induced thrombocytopenia than warfarin. It is a fallback when warfarin is declined, not the preferred strategy at this dose. (Source: RANZCOG: Cardiac disease in pregnancy)

options.text: Stop the warfarin and commence a direct oral anticoagulant, which avoids both the teratogenic risk and the need for injections
options.rationale: Direct oral anticoagulants are contraindicated with mechanical valves in any patient because of unacceptable thrombotic event rates in trial data, and they are additionally not recommended in pregnancy. This option is unsafe on two independent grounds. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

explanation.summary: Anticoagulation for a mechanical heart valve in pregnancy is a decision in which every option trades maternal against foetal risk, and it is the clearest example in obstetric medicine of competing guidance requiring an explicit choice. Warfarin provides the most reliable protection against valve thrombosis but crosses the placenta and causes an embryopathy of nasal hypoplasia and stippled epiphyses when taken between six and twelve weeks, with the risk being dose dependent and low at daily requirements at or below about 5 mg. Low molecular weight heparin does not cross the placenta but achieves less consistent anticoagulation of a prosthetic valve, and if used it must be therapeutic, twice daily and adjusted to peak anti-factor Xa levels around 1.0 to 1.2 units per millilitre rather than given at fixed dose. Direct oral anticoagulants are contraindicated with mechanical valves irrespective of pregnancy. The practical approach is warfarin continuation through the first trimester when the dose is low, a planned switch to therapeutic heparin from about 36 weeks to allow safe regional analgesia and birth, and management throughout by a multidisciplinary team, with the woman's informed preference documented because valve thrombosis carries a maternal mortality far exceeding the foetal risk being avoided.
key_points: Warfarin embryopathy risk is dose dependent and low at daily doses of 5 mg or less
The vulnerable window for embryopathy is approximately six to twelve weeks gestation
Heparin for a mechanical valve must be therapeutic, twice daily and anti-factor Xa adjusted
Direct oral anticoagulants are contraindicated with mechanical valves in any patient
No interruption of anticoagulation is acceptable, and aspirin is not a substitute
explanation.pearls: Switch a woman with a mechanical valve from warfarin to therapeutic low molecular weight heparin at around 36 weeks, because delivering while the foetus is warfarinised risks fatal neonatal intracranial haemorrhage during birth even when the maternal international normalised ratio is in range.

subtopic_detail: first line treatment for repetitive hair pulling causing visible loss and concealment
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 22 year old university student who has worn a beanie indoors at every consultation this year. Today she tells you she has been pulling out her own hair since she was fourteen, mostly while studying or watching television, and has a bare patch at her crown that she covers.

She describes rising tension before pulling and relief afterwards. She does not believe her appearance is defective in any other way and does not check mirrors or seek cosmetic opinions. She has no intrusive contamination or harm thoughts and performs no washing, checking or ordering rituals. She has tried to stop many times and feels ashamed. On examination there is an irregular area of incomplete hair loss at the vertex with hairs of varying lengths and no scaling, no scarring, no erythema and no broken hair fluorescence. Her thyroid function and iron studies are within normal limits.

data_table.Examination: Irregular area of incomplete alopecia at the vertex with hairs of varying lengths; no scaling, scarring, erythema or pustules; remainder of scalp and eyebrows normal
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid function and iron studies within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line treatment?

options.text: Commence low dose olanzapine at night and review her pulling frequency and any weight change after six weeks
options.rationale: Antipsychotics have some evidence as augmentation in refractory cases but carry metabolic burden that is hard to justify as an initial step in a young woman. They sit well behind behavioural therapy in the treatment sequence. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Advise her that this is a habit that will settle with time and suggest keeping her hands occupied during television and study
options.rationale: Trichotillomania is a chronic condition with a waxing and waning course that rarely remits without treatment, and this advice offers a fragment of a therapeutic technique without the structure that makes it work. It also risks her hearing her distress as trivial. (Source: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders

options.text: Refer her for habit reversal training with awareness training and a competing response to the urge to pull
options.rationale: Hair pulling with premonitory tension and subsequent relief, without obsessions or appearance related beliefs, is trichotillomania, for which habit reversal training within a behavioural package has the strongest evidence and outperforms any medication. Awareness training addresses the automatic pulling that occurs during sedentary activities. (Source: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders

options.text: Commence a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor titrated to the higher end of the dose range over eight weeks
options.rationale: Serotonin reuptake inhibitors are effective in obsessive compulsive disorder but trials in trichotillomania have been largely negative, which is one of the clearest pharmacological differences between these related conditions. They remain useful for a comorbid depressive or anxiety disorder. (Source: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Obsessive compulsive and related disorders

options.text: Refer her to a dermatologist for a scalp biopsy and trial of a potent topical corticosteroid to the affected area
options.rationale: The clinical picture of irregular alopecia with hairs of differing lengths and intact skin is characteristic of pulling, whereas alopecia areata gives smooth round patches with exclamation mark hairs and tinea capitis gives scaling with broken hairs. Biopsy and topical steroid treat neither the behaviour nor its cause. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology)

explanation.summary: Trichotillomania sits within the obsessive compulsive and related disorders but differs from obsessive compulsive disorder in both phenomenology and treatment response. Pulling is preceded by mounting tension or an urge and followed by relief or gratification, and it occurs in both a focused mode, where the person is aware and often distressed, and an automatic mode during sedentary activities such as reading, studying or screen time. There are no obsessions, and the absence of appearance related preoccupation distinguishes it from body dysmorphic disorder, in which hair removal is driven by a belief that the hair itself is defective. The dermatological differential matters because irregular patches with hairs of varying length and normal underlying skin point to pulling, whereas smooth patches with exclamation mark hairs suggest alopecia areata and scaling with broken hairs suggests tinea capitis. Habit reversal training, usually delivered within a broader behavioural package, is first line, and unlike obsessive compulsive disorder the condition responds poorly to serotonin reuptake inhibitors, with N-acetylcysteine having modest supporting evidence as an adjunct.
key_points: Premonitory tension with relief after pulling is the defining phenomenology
Automatic pulling during sedentary activity requires awareness training to address
Serotonin reuptake inhibitors work in obsessive compulsive disorder but not in trichotillomania
Irregular patches with varying hair lengths and normal skin distinguish it dermatologically
Habit reversal training within a behavioural package is first line treatment
explanation.pearls: Ask specifically about trichophagia, because swallowing pulled hair can form a trichobezoar that extends into the small bowel as Rapunzel syndrome and presents with obstruction, and it requires surgical rather than psychiatric management.
