subtopic_detail: deciding whether to raise or lower corticosteroid when psychosis emerges during treatment of an autoimmune disease
stem:
You are the consultation liaison psychiatry registrar asked to see a 24 year old woman on the renal ward. She was admitted eleven days ago with systemic lupus erythematosus and biopsy proven class IV nephritis, and was commenced on prednisolone 60 mg daily nine days ago after three pulses of methylprednisolone.

Over the last two days she has become perplexed, believes the nursing staff are substituting her medication, and has been seen responding to voices. Her treating team is divided between reducing the corticosteroid and increasing it. She has a new right sided pronator drift and two brief episodes of right arm jerking witnessed overnight. Temperature 37.8 degrees Celsius with other vital signs within normal limits. Complement C3 and C4 are falling, double stranded deoxyribonucleic acid antibody titre is rising, and her creatinine has risen from 118 to 164 micromol/L (45 to 90). Cerebrospinal fluid shows 22 lymphocytes per microlitre with a raised protein, a normal glucose and a negative Gram stain.

data_table.Vital signs: Temperature 37.8 degrees Celsius with pulse, blood pressure, respiratory rate and oxygen saturation within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Perplexed with persecutory beliefs and auditory hallucinations; new right sided pronator drift; two witnessed brief episodes of right arm jerking; no neck stiffness
data_table.Investigations: Complement C3 and C4 falling; double stranded deoxyribonucleic acid antibody titre rising; creatinine risen from 118 to 164 micromol/L (45 to 90); cerebrospinal fluid 22 lymphocytes per microlitre with raised protein, normal glucose and negative Gram stain

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Reduce the prednisolone dose progressively and commence olanzapine, attributing the presentation to corticosteroid induced psychosis
options.rationale: Corticosteroid induced psychosis is the tempting alternative and does typically appear within the first two weeks at doses above 40 mg daily, but it produces mood disturbance and psychosis without focal signs, seizures or cerebrospinal fluid pleocytosis. Reducing immunosuppression during active nephritis and cerebral disease risks irreversible organ damage. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association)

options.text: Cease the corticosteroid entirely and commence intravenous aciclovir empirically for suspected herpes simplex encephalitis
options.rationale: Viral encephalitis must be excluded with cerebrospinal fluid polymerase chain reaction and empirical aciclovir is reasonable while that is pending, but abruptly ceasing corticosteroid in a woman on nine days of high dose therapy risks adrenal crisis and a lupus flare. Cessation and escalation are different decisions and only one is safe here. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Commence haloperidol and lorazepam for the psychotic symptoms and defer any change to her immunosuppressive regimen
options.rationale: Symptomatic treatment alone leaves an active inflammatory cerebral process untreated, and neuropsychiatric lupus with seizures and focal signs carries a real risk of permanent deficit. The psychiatric treatment is necessary but is not sufficient on its own. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association)

options.text: Arrange urgent electroconvulsive therapy for the psychotic presentation and continue her current corticosteroid dose unchanged
options.rationale: Electroconvulsive therapy is used for catatonia and severe refractory affective psychosis, and this woman has an organic cerebral process with seizures and a focal deficit. Inducing seizures in active cerebral lupus without treating the inflammation would be unsafe. (Source: RANZCP: Electroconvulsive therapy)

options.text: Escalate immunosuppression after excluding infection, and treat the psychotic symptoms symptomatically while monitoring neurologically
options.rationale: Falling complement, a rising double stranded deoxyribonucleic acid titre, worsening nephritis, focal neurological signs, seizures and an inflammatory cerebrospinal fluid all indicate active neuropsychiatric lupus rather than a drug effect, and that requires more immunosuppression rather than less. Antipsychotic therapy manages the symptoms while the immunological treatment addresses the cause. (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association)

explanation.summary: Psychosis emerging in a patient recently started on high dose corticosteroid for an autoimmune disease creates a genuine dilemma, because the two leading explanations demand opposite interventions and choosing wrongly causes harm in either direction. Corticosteroid induced neuropsychiatric effects are dose related, occur most often above prednisolone 40 mg daily, typically begin within the first fortnight, and produce affective disturbance, insomnia and sometimes psychosis without focal neurological signs, seizures or cerebrospinal fluid abnormality. Neuropsychiatric systemic lupus erythematosus, by contrast, tends to occur alongside evidence of systemic disease activity such as falling complement, rising double stranded deoxyribonucleic acid antibodies and worsening nephritis, and is accompanied by focal deficits, seizures, an inflammatory cerebrospinal fluid or abnormal neuroimaging. Infection must always be excluded first in an immunosuppressed patient, since central nervous system infection presents similarly and would be worsened by escalation. When the evidence points to active lupus, the correct response is more immunosuppression, commonly with pulsed methylprednisolone followed by cyclophosphamide or rituximab, with antipsychotic therapy used symptomatically alongside it.
key_points: The two explanations require opposite treatments, so the discriminators must be sought explicitly
Corticosteroid psychosis lacks focal signs, seizures and cerebrospinal fluid pleocytosis
Falling complement with rising anti-double stranded deoxyribonucleic acid indicates active disease
Exclude central nervous system infection before escalating immunosuppression
Active neuropsychiatric lupus is treated with escalation, not reduction, of immunosuppression
explanation.pearls: Antiphospholipid antibodies should be measured in any patient with neuropsychiatric lupus, because thrombotic rather than inflammatory mechanisms require anticoagulation instead of immunosuppression and the two can coexist in the same patient.

subtopic_detail: diagnosis and therapy for prolonged fever with hepatitis in an abattoir worker
stem:
You are the general practitioner in a regional town seeing a 38 year old man with three weeks of fever, drenching sweats, severe retro-orbital headache and profound fatigue. He has lost 5 kg. He works on the kill floor of the local abattoir and helped with a sheep shearing weekend a month ago. He has not travelled overseas.

He has taken two courses of amoxicillin from an after hours service without benefit. Examination shows a temperature of 38.7 degrees Celsius with other vital signs within normal limits, a tender liver edge 2 cm below the costal margin, no lymphadenopathy, no rash and no murmur. Alanine aminotransferase is 186 U/L (less than 40), alkaline phosphatase 168 U/L (30 to 110), bilirubin within normal limits, white cell count 6.8 x10^9/L (4.0 to 11.0), platelets 128 x10^9/L (150 to 400) and C-reactive protein 84 mg/L (less than 5). Chest radiograph and two sets of blood cultures are negative.

data_table.Vital signs: Temperature 38.7 degrees Celsius with pulse, blood pressure, respiratory rate and oxygen saturation within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Tender liver edge 2 cm below costal margin; no lymphadenopathy, rash, splinter haemorrhages or murmur
data_table.Investigations: Alanine aminotransferase 186 U/L (less than 40); alkaline phosphatase 168 U/L (30 to 110); bilirubin within normal limits; white cell count 6.8 x10^9/L (4.0 to 11.0); platelets 128 x10^9/L (150 to 400); C-reactive protein 84 mg/L (less than 5); chest radiograph normal; two sets of blood cultures negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Repeat blood cultures while febrile and commence intravenous ceftriaxone empirically pending those culture results
options.rationale: Coxiella burnetii is an obligate intracellular organism that will not grow in standard blood culture bottles, so repeat cultures will again be negative. Cephalosporins have no activity against it. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Send paired phase I and phase II serology and commence oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for a two week course
options.rationale: A prolonged febrile illness with hepatitis, thrombocytopenia and a normal white cell count in someone with intensive livestock exposure is Coxiella burnetii infection, which is not detected on routine blood culture and does not respond to beta-lactams. Doxycycline is the treatment of choice and serology distinguishes acute from persistent infection. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Send Brucella serology and commence oral rifampicin with doxycycline for a six week combination course
options.rationale: Brucellosis produces a very similar undulant febrile illness with hepatitis and is a reasonable differential, but it is exceptionally rare in Australia outside feral pig hunters and returned travellers. Its treatment is longer and combination based, so committing to it without supporting exposure is inappropriate. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Send hepatitis A, B and C serology and manage him supportively pending the results of that viral screen
options.rationale: Viral hepatitis should be tested for, but the transaminase rise here is modest and accompanied by three weeks of high fever, sweats and weight loss, which acute viral hepatitis does not usually sustain. Supportive management alone leaves a treatable bacterial infection untreated. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Arrange a computed tomography scan of the chest, abdomen and pelvis to investigate a possible occult lymphoproliferative disorder
options.rationale: Imaging for occult malignancy is a reasonable step in a fever of unknown origin once infective causes with a clear exposure history have been excluded. Ordering it before testing the single most likely occupational diagnosis inverts the sequence. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Q fever)

explanation.summary: Q fever is caused by Coxiella burnetii, which is shed in very high concentration in the birth products, urine and faeces of cattle, sheep and goats and is acquired by inhaling contaminated aerosols or dust, making abattoir workers, shearers, farmers and veterinarians the classical risk groups. Acute infection presents as an undifferentiated febrile illness with prominent headache, often retro-orbital, sweats and myalgia, frequently with a hepatitis and a normal or low white cell count with mild thrombocytopenia, and it may present as atypical pneumonia. The organism is intracellular and does not grow in routine blood culture, so serology using phase I and phase II antibodies is the diagnostic test, with a rising phase II titre indicating acute infection and a high phase I titre suggesting persistent focalised infection such as endocarditis. Doxycycline is the treatment of choice for acute disease, and persistent infection requires prolonged doxycycline with hydroxychloroquine under specialist supervision. A vaccine is available in Australia and is recommended for at risk occupations, but it requires pre-vaccination skin testing and serology because vaccinating someone with prior exposure causes severe local reactions.
key_points: Livestock aerosol exposure in abattoir workers, shearers and farmers is the key history
Hepatitis with a normal white cell count and mild thrombocytopenia is typical
The organism is intracellular and does not grow in routine blood culture
Phase I and phase II serology separates acute from persistent focalised infection
Doxycycline is first line; beta-lactams are ineffective
explanation.pearls: Q fever vaccination in Australia requires pre-vaccination skin testing and serology, because giving the vaccine to someone with prior exposure produces severe local and systemic hypersensitivity reactions including sterile abscess formation.

subtopic_detail: treatment of an acute crystal arthritis with rhomboid crystals in a patient with renal impairment
stem:
You are the doctor on a medical ward. A 78 year old woman admitted four days ago with community acquired pneumonia has developed a hot, swollen, exquisitely painful left knee overnight. She has never had joint problems before and does not drink alcohol.

Temperature 37.6 degrees Celsius with other vital signs within normal limits. The knee is warm with a moderate effusion and she resists all movement. A plain radiograph shows a thin line of calcification within the meniscal cartilage and the hyaline articular cartilage. Joint aspiration yields cloudy yellow fluid with 22 000 white cells per microlitre, predominantly neutrophils, a negative Gram stain, and rhomboid crystals showing weak positive birefringence under polarised light. Her creatinine is 168 micromol/L with an estimated glomerular filtration rate of 26 mL/min/1.73m2, and her serum urate is 0.32 mmol/L (0.15 to 0.45).

data_table.Vital signs: Temperature 37.6 degrees Celsius with pulse, blood pressure, respiratory rate and oxygen saturation within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Warm left knee with moderate effusion, marked tenderness and resistance to passive movement; no overlying skin breach or cellulitis
data_table.Investigations: Knee radiograph shows linear calcification in meniscal and hyaline cartilage; synovial fluid 22 000 white cells per microlitre predominantly neutrophils, Gram stain negative, rhomboid crystals with weak positive birefringence; creatinine 168 micromol/L with estimated glomerular filtration rate 26 mL/min/1.73m2; serum urate 0.32 mmol/L (0.15 to 0.45)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment while cultures are pending?

options.text: Commence a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug at full dose with a proton pump inhibitor for gastric protection
options.rationale: Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs are first line in younger patients with normal renal function but are contraindicated here, where they would worsen an already reduced glomerular filtration rate and add gastrointestinal and cardiovascular risk in a 78 year old. Gastric protection does not address the renal hazard. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Commence allopurinol at a low dose and titrate upward against a target serum urate below 0.36 mmol/L
options.rationale: Allopurinol lowers urate and has no effect on calcium pyrophosphate crystals, and her urate is within the reference range so gout is not the diagnosis. Starting urate lowering therapy during an acute attack of any crystal arthritis can also prolong it. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology)

options.text: Commence intravenous flucloxacillin for presumed septic arthritis and arrange arthroscopic washout of the joint today
options.rationale: Septic arthritis must be considered and is the reason cultures were sent, but a negative Gram stain with identified crystals and a synovial white cell count of 22 000 per microlitre favours crystal disease, since septic counts are usually above 50 000 per microlitre. Committing to washout before culture results in a patient with an alternative explanation is disproportionate. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Perform an intra-articular corticosteroid injection into the knee once the synovial fluid culture has been reported as negative
options.rationale: Weakly positively birefringent rhomboid crystals with cartilage calcification identify calcium pyrophosphate crystal arthritis, and intra-articular corticosteroid is the preferred treatment in an older patient with an estimated glomerular filtration rate of 26 mL/min/1.73m2 because it avoids systemic drug exposure. Waiting for a negative culture is appropriate since injecting a septic joint would be harmful. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology)

options.text: Commence oral colchicine at a loading dose followed by twice daily maintenance until the joint symptoms have settled
options.rationale: Colchicine is effective in crystal arthritis but is renally cleared, and at this level of kidney function it accumulates and causes diarrhoea, myelosuppression and neuromyopathy. Dose reduction is required and even then it is a poorer choice than a local injection. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

explanation.summary: Calcium pyrophosphate crystal arthritis, historically called pseudogout, typically affects older adults and is frequently precipitated by intercurrent illness, surgery, trauma or metabolic disturbance, which is why it commonly appears several days into a hospital admission for something else. The knee and wrist are the joints most often involved, and chondrocalcinosis on plain radiography, seen as a thin line of calcification within fibrocartilage and hyaline cartilage, supports the diagnosis although it can be present without symptoms. Synovial fluid analysis is the definitive test, showing rhomboid or rod shaped crystals with weak positive birefringence, in contrast to the needle shaped, strongly negatively birefringent crystals of monosodium urate. The presence of crystals never excludes coexisting infection, so fluid must always be sent for Gram stain and culture and the two can occur together. Treatment of the acute attack is with intra-articular corticosteroid, a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug, colchicine or systemic corticosteroid, with the choice driven by renal function, age and comorbidity, and recurrent attacks should prompt screening for haemochromatosis, hyperparathyroidism, hypophosphatasia and hypomagnesaemia.
key_points: Rhomboid crystals with weak positive birefringence distinguish this from monosodium urate
Chondrocalcinosis on radiography supports but does not confirm the diagnosis
Intercurrent illness or surgery is a classical trigger in hospital inpatients
Crystals do not exclude infection; always culture the fluid
Choose treatment by renal function and comorbidity rather than by default
explanation.pearls: Recurrent calcium pyrophosphate arthritis under the age of about 60 should prompt screening for haemochromatosis, primary hyperparathyroidism, hypomagnesaemia and hypophosphatasia, since these metabolic associations are treatable and are missed if the attack is simply managed symptomatically.

subtopic_detail: interpreting visible haematuria occurring at the same time as a sore throat rather than weeks later
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 23 year old man who noticed his urine turned the colour of dark tea yesterday. He developed a sore throat two days ago and the urine change began on the second day of the throat symptoms. He recalls a similar episode of dark urine two years ago during a chest infection, which cleared within a week and was not investigated.

He has no dysuria, no frequency, no flank pain and no recent exercise or trauma. Blood pressure 138/86 mmHg with other vital signs within normal limits. There is no oedema, no rash and no joint swelling. Urine microscopy shows numerous dysmorphic red cells with red cell casts. Urine protein to creatinine ratio is 68 mg/mmol. Creatinine is 96 micromol/L with an estimated glomerular filtration rate of 88 mL/min/1.73m2. Complement C3 and C4 are within normal limits, antinuclear antibody and antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody are negative, and an antistreptolysin O titre is not raised.

data_table.Vital signs: Blood pressure 138/86 mmHg with other vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: No peripheral or periorbital oedema; no rash or purpura; no synovitis; pharynx mildly injected
data_table.Investigations: Urine microscopy shows dysmorphic red cells with red cell casts; urine protein to creatinine ratio 68 mg/mmol; creatinine 96 micromol/L with estimated glomerular filtration rate 88 mL/min/1.73m2; complement C3 and C4 within normal limits; antinuclear antibody and antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody negative; antistreptolysin O titre not raised

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Commence an angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitor targeting a blood pressure below 130/80 mmHg and refer to nephrology
options.rationale: Visible haematuria occurring at the same time as a mucosal infection, with dysmorphic cells and red cell casts, normal complement and a negative autoimmune screen, is characteristic of immunoglobulin A nephropathy, and renin-angiotensin blockade with strict blood pressure control is the foundation of treatment. Nephrology referral establishes whether biopsy and additional therapy are needed given the proteinuria. (Source: KHA-CARI: Glomerulonephritis)

options.text: Prescribe phenoxymethylpenicillin for the pharyngitis and repeat the urinalysis in four weeks once the infection has resolved
options.rationale: Antibiotic treatment of the throat does not alter the renal process, and repeating urinalysis alone in a man with red cell casts and significant proteinuria under-investigates established glomerular disease. The haematuria will settle spontaneously and give false reassurance. (Source: KHA-CARI: Glomerulonephritis)

options.text: Arrange a computed tomography urogram and cystoscopy to exclude a urothelial or renal tract source for the visible haematuria
options.rationale: Urological imaging and cystoscopy are the pathway for painless visible haematuria in an older patient or where the bleeding is non-glomerular. Dysmorphic red cells with casts and proteinuria localise the bleeding to the glomerulus and make a urological source very unlikely. (Source: KHA-CARI: Glomerulonephritis)

options.text: Commence oral prednisolone at 1 mg/kg daily and arrange nephrology review once the corticosteroid course is completed
options.rationale: Corticosteroids are considered only for patients who remain at high risk of progression despite maximal supportive therapy, and they carry substantial infective and metabolic toxicity. Starting them before optimised blood pressure and renin-angiotensin blockade reverses the accepted treatment order. (Source: KHA-CARI: Glomerulonephritis)

options.text: Reassure him that this represents a benign familial thin basement membrane condition and arrange annual urinalysis review
options.rationale: Thin basement membrane nephropathy causes persistent microscopic haematuria without significant proteinuria and rarely produces visible haematuria linked to infection. A protein to creatinine ratio of 68 mg/mmol is well beyond what that diagnosis explains. (Source: KHA-CARI: Glomerulonephritis)

explanation.summary: Immunoglobulin A nephropathy is the commonest primary glomerulonephritis worldwide and classically presents in young adults with visible haematuria occurring within one to two days of a mucosal infection, most often pharyngitis. This synpharyngitic timing is the key discriminator from post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis, which follows a streptococcal infection after a latent period of one to three weeks and is accompanied by a low C3 and a raised antistreptolysin O titre. Dysmorphic red cells and red cell casts confirm a glomerular source and make urological investigation unnecessary in a young patient. Prognosis is driven by the degree of proteinuria, the blood pressure and the glomerular filtration rate at presentation, and treatment begins with optimised supportive care including renin-angiotensin system blockade titrated to maximum tolerated dose, strict blood pressure targets, sodium restriction and cardiovascular risk management. Immunosuppression and newer targeted agents are reserved for those with persistent proteinuria above about 0.75 to 1 g per day despite several months of optimised supportive therapy, and renal biopsy is used to confirm the diagnosis and grade the histological risk.
key_points: Haematuria concurrent with the infection suggests immunoglobulin A nephropathy
A latent period of one to three weeks with low C3 suggests post-streptococcal disease instead
Dysmorphic red cells and red cell casts localise bleeding to the glomerulus
Renin-angiotensin blockade with strict blood pressure control is the foundation of treatment
Proteinuria, blood pressure and filtration rate at presentation drive prognosis
explanation.pearls: Proteinuria above roughly 1 g per day sustained after several months of maximally tolerated renin-angiotensin blockade is the threshold at which additional immunosuppressive or targeted therapy is considered in immunoglobulin A nephropathy, so quantifying the protein excretion matters more than the visible haematuria that brought the patient in.

subtopic_detail: workup of an isolated raised alkaline phosphatase with localised bone pain and deformity
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 71 year old man who has had a deep ache in his right shin for eight months, worse at night and present at rest. He mentions that his hats have become tighter over the last two years and that he has noticed some hearing loss on the right.

He is otherwise well and takes no medication. On examination the right tibia is bowed anteriorly and feels warm compared with the left. Alkaline phosphatase is 684 U/L (30 to 110), with gamma glutamyl transferase, alanine aminotransferase and bilirubin all within normal limits. Corrected calcium is 2.36 mmol/L (2.15 to 2.60), phosphate is within normal limits, parathyroid hormone is within normal limits, 25-hydroxyvitamin D is 68 nmol/L (50 to 150) and creatinine is within normal limits. A radiograph of the tibia shows cortical thickening, coarse trabeculation and an area of lucency with a flame shaped advancing edge.

data_table.Examination: Anterior bowing of the right tibia with overlying warmth; increased skull circumference reported; reduced hearing on the right
data_table.Investigations: Alkaline phosphatase 684 U/L (30 to 110); gamma glutamyl transferase, alanine aminotransferase and bilirubin within normal limits; corrected calcium 2.36 mmol/L (2.15 to 2.60); phosphate, parathyroid hormone and creatinine within normal limits; 25-hydroxyvitamin D 68 nmol/L (50 to 150); tibial radiograph shows cortical thickening, coarse trabeculation and a flame shaped lucent advancing front

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence high dose colecalciferol with oral calcium supplementation and recheck the bone profile after twelve weeks
options.rationale: Vitamin D deficiency causes osteomalacia, which raises alkaline phosphatase but produces a low or low normal calcium, a low phosphate and a raised parathyroid hormone. His vitamin D is adequate and his parathyroid hormone is normal, which excludes that mechanism. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Commence oral denosumab equivalent antiresorptive therapy every six months and monitor the alkaline phosphatase annually
options.rationale: Denosumab is given subcutaneously rather than orally and is not established therapy for this condition, where potent nitrogen containing bisphosphonates have the evidence base. It also carries a risk of rebound bone turnover when stopped. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Arrange a radionuclide bone scan to define the extent of disease and give a single intravenous zoledronic acid infusion
options.rationale: A markedly raised alkaline phosphatase of bony origin with a normal liver panel, bone pain, bowing deformity and the characteristic radiographic advancing front establishes Paget disease of bone, and a bone scan maps the distribution including sites that are clinically silent but at risk. A single zoledronic acid infusion produces prolonged biochemical remission and relieves the pain. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Repeat the alkaline phosphatase with liver function tests in three months and investigate further only if it continues to rise
options.rationale: Watchful waiting is reasonable for a mildly raised alkaline phosphatase of uncertain origin, but a level six times the upper limit with a normal gamma glutamyl transferase and characteristic radiology already establishes the diagnosis. Delay allows further deformity and hearing loss to accrue. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Arrange a bone biopsy of the tibial lesion to exclude an underlying primary bone malignancy before commencing any treatment
options.rationale: Biopsy is indicated when a lytic lesion has features suspicious for sarcoma such as cortical destruction, a soft tissue mass or rapidly worsening pain, which are absent here. The radiographic appearance described is the typical advancing resorption front of the disease itself. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Paget disease of bone)
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Paget disease of bone

explanation.summary: Paget disease of bone is a focal disorder of accelerated and disorganised bone remodelling that affects older adults and most commonly involves the pelvis, spine, femur, tibia and skull. Many cases are found incidentally through an isolated raised alkaline phosphatase, and the first step is to confirm that the enzyme is of bony rather than hepatic origin, which a normal gamma glutamyl transferase and normal transaminases achieve. The differential for a raised alkaline phosphatase with bone pain includes osteomalacia, which is distinguished by a low or low normal calcium, low phosphate, raised parathyroid hormone and low vitamin D, and metastatic bone disease, which produces destructive rather than expansile changes. Radiographic features of Paget disease include cortical thickening, coarse trabeculation, bone expansion and bowing, with a flame shaped or blade of grass lucent advancing front in long bones. Treatment with a potent bisphosphonate, usually a single zoledronic acid infusion, relieves bone pain and normalises turnover for years, and it is indicated for symptomatic disease or for asymptomatic disease at sites where complications such as deafness, nerve compression, fracture or joint destruction would be serious.
key_points: Confirm the bony origin of a raised alkaline phosphatase with a normal gamma glutamyl transferase
Normal calcium, phosphate, parathyroid hormone and vitamin D exclude osteomalacia
The flame shaped advancing lucent front is characteristic in long bones
Bone scan maps disease extent including clinically silent but risky sites
A single zoledronic acid infusion gives prolonged biochemical and symptomatic remission
explanation.pearls: New, severe or rapidly escalating pain in a previously stable pagetic bone, particularly with a soft tissue mass, should raise osteosarcoma, which complicates well under one per cent of cases but carries a very poor prognosis and requires urgent imaging and biopsy rather than escalation of bisphosphonate therapy.

sources.label: BMJ Best Practice: Paget disease of bone

subtopic_detail: treating a painless genital ulcer with a positive treponemal screen and reactive rapid plasma reagin
stem:
You are the doctor in a sexual health clinic seeing a 31 year old man who noticed a sore on his penis ten days ago. It does not hurt and he only sought review because it has not healed. He has had three male partners in the past six months and uses condoms inconsistently. He takes tenofovir with emtricitabine as pre-exposure prophylaxis and his last human immunodeficiency virus test six weeks ago was negative.

On examination there is a single 1 cm ulcer on the coronal sulcus with a clean indurated base and a rolled edge, and it is not tender to touch. There are firm, non-tender, mobile inguinal nodes bilaterally. There is no rash on the trunk, palms or soles, no oral lesion and no alopecia. Treponemal enzyme immunoassay is reactive, rapid plasma reagin titre is 1 in 32, and a swab of the ulcer base is positive for Treponema pallidum on polymerase chain reaction. Repeat human immunodeficiency virus serology and nucleic acid testing are negative.

data_table.Examination: Single 1 cm indurated painless ulcer with a clean base at the coronal sulcus; firm non-tender mobile bilateral inguinal lymphadenopathy; no truncal, palmar or plantar rash; no oral lesions
data_table.Investigations: Treponemal enzyme immunoassay reactive; rapid plasma reagin titre 1 in 32; ulcer base polymerase chain reaction positive for Treponema pallidum; human immunodeficiency virus serology and nucleic acid testing negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: Three weekly intramuscular doses of benzathine benzylpenicillin 1.8 g, with contact tracing and repeat serology at three months
options.rationale: Three weekly doses are the regimen for late latent syphilis, syphilis of unknown duration and tertiary disease, where slower treponemal replication requires prolonged treponemicidal levels. Applying it to early infection means two unnecessary injections. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: A fourteen day course of oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily, with contact tracing and repeat serology at three months
options.rationale: Doxycycline for fourteen days is the recommended alternative for a patient with genuine penicillin hypersensitivity, and it requires good adherence and closer serological follow up. It is second line where penicillin can be given. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: A single intramuscular dose of ceftriaxone 500 mg with a single oral dose of azithromycin 1 g, and contact tracing
options.rationale: This is empirical therapy for gonorrhoea and chlamydia, and azithromycin resistance in Treponema pallidum is widespread in Australia so it should not be relied upon. Concurrent infections should be tested for and treated, but this regimen does not treat the confirmed diagnosis. (Source: ASHM: Australian STI management guidelines)

options.text: A ten day course of oral valaciclovir 500 mg twice daily, with contact tracing and repeat serology at three months
options.rationale: Antiviral therapy treats genital herpes, which characteristically produces painful grouped vesicles progressing to shallow tender ulcers with tender lymphadenopathy. The painless indurated ulcer with non-tender nodes and a positive treponemal polymerase chain reaction points elsewhere. (Source: ASHM: Australian STI management guidelines)

options.text: A single intramuscular dose of benzathine benzylpenicillin 1.8 g, with contact tracing and repeat serology at three months
options.rationale: A painless indurated ulcer with confirmed Treponema pallidum and a reactive treponemal test is primary syphilis, which is treated with a single intramuscular dose of long acting benzathine benzylpenicillin. Contact tracing covers partners from the three months preceding symptom onset, and serial rapid plasma reagin titres document the response. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Syphilis has re-emerged in Australia with rising rates among men who have sex with men and a concerning increase in heterosexual and congenital infection, so any genital ulcer warrants testing regardless of the perceived risk profile. Primary syphilis presents as a chancre appearing about three weeks after exposure, classically single, painless, indurated with a clean base, and accompanied by firm non-tender regional lymphadenopathy, which distinguishes it from the painful vesicles and ulcers of herpes simplex and the painful ragged ulcer of chancroid. Diagnosis in Australian practice combines a treponemal screening immunoassay, a non-treponemal rapid plasma reagin titre for staging and monitoring, and direct detection from the lesion by polymerase chain reaction. Treatment of early syphilis, meaning primary, secondary or early latent infection of under two years duration, is a single intramuscular dose of benzathine benzylpenicillin, while late latent disease or infection of unknown duration requires three weekly doses. Management is incomplete without contact tracing, testing for concurrent sexually transmissible infections including human immunodeficiency virus, and serological follow up demonstrating a fourfold fall in the rapid plasma reagin titre.
key_points: A painless indurated ulcer with non-tender nodes distinguishes chancre from herpes
Early syphilis under two years duration requires a single benzathine penicillin dose
Late latent or unknown duration infection requires three weekly doses
Azithromycin resistance is widespread and it should not be used
Follow up requires a fourfold fall in rapid plasma reagin titre and full contact tracing
explanation.pearls: Warn the patient about the Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction, a self-limiting fever, rigors and myalgia occurring within hours of the first penicillin dose from treponemal lysis, since it is commonly mistaken for penicillin allergy and leads to inappropriate avoidance of the best treatment.

subtopic_detail: empirical therapy for cavitating pneumonia in a diabetic patient during the northern wet season
stem:
You are the medical registrar in a Northern Territory regional hospital in February. A 54 year old man is admitted with five days of fever, productive cough and pleuritic chest pain. He has type 2 diabetes with a glycated haemoglobin of 9.8 per cent and drinks heavily. He works as a landscaper and has been digging in flooded ground after recent heavy rain.

Pulse rate 118 per minute, blood pressure 96/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 per minute, SpO2 90 per cent on room air, temperature 39.1 degrees Celsius. Chest examination reveals right sided bronchial breathing. Chest radiograph shows a right upper lobe consolidation containing two thin walled cavities, and computed tomography of the abdomen performed for pain shows three small hypodense splenic lesions. White cell count is 19.6 x10^9/L (4.0 to 11.0), creatinine 142 micromol/L (60 to 110), lactate 3.4 mmol/L (less than 2.0) and blood cultures are flagging as positive with Gram negative bacilli.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 118 per minute, blood pressure 96/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 per minute, SpO2 90 per cent on room air, temperature 39.1 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Right sided bronchial breathing with dullness to percussion; no skin lesions; no meningism
data_table.Investigations: Chest radiograph shows right upper lobe consolidation with two thin walled cavities; computed tomography abdomen shows three small hypodense splenic lesions; white cell count 19.6 x10^9/L (4.0 to 11.0); creatinine 142 micromol/L (60 to 110); lactate 3.4 mmol/L (less than 2.0); glycated haemoglobin 9.8 per cent; blood cultures positive with Gram negative bacilli

lead_in: What is the most appropriate empirical antimicrobial therapy?

options.text: Intravenous liposomal amphotericin B, treating for an invasive fungal infection given his poorly controlled diabetes
options.rationale: Invasive fungal disease is a consideration in poorly controlled diabetes but typically involves the sinuses, orbit or brain in mucormycosis rather than producing this pattern. Gram negative bacilli in the blood cultures direct therapy away from antifungal cover. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Intravenous meropenem, with a plan for prolonged oral eradication therapy after the intensive intravenous phase
options.rationale: Cavitating pneumonia with splenic abscesses and Gram negative bacteraemia in a diabetic man with soil and water exposure during the wet season in northern Australia is melioidosis until proven otherwise, and Burkholderia pseudomallei is intrinsically resistant to many agents. Meropenem is preferred over ceftazidime in severe disease with septic shock, and the mandatory eradication phase prevents the relapse that follows inadequate treatment. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Intravenous benzylpenicillin with oral doxycycline, escalating if there is no clinical response over the next 48 hours
options.rationale: This is the standard regimen for moderate community acquired pneumonia and would be reasonable in a temperate setting without these risk features. Burkholderia pseudomallei is intrinsically resistant to penicillin and the delay would be measured against a high mortality. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Intravenous flucloxacillin with intravenous gentamicin, covering staphylococcal cavitating pneumonia with metastatic seeding
options.rationale: Staphylococcus aureus is a genuine cause of cavitating pneumonia with distant abscesses and is the closest differential, but the blood cultures show Gram negative bacilli which excludes it. Burkholderia pseudomallei is also intrinsically resistant to aminoglycosides, so this regimen would provide no effective cover. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Intravenous piperacillin with tazobactam and a single dose of intravenous gentamicin, reviewing once susceptibilities return
options.rationale: This is a common empirical choice for Gram negative sepsis and has some activity against Burkholderia pseudomallei, but it is not the recommended agent and outcome data favour a carbapenem or ceftazidime. Adding gentamicin contributes nothing against this organism and risks further renal injury. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Melioidosis is caused by Burkholderia pseudomallei, an environmental saprophyte of soil and surface water across northern Australia and Southeast Asia, and cases cluster sharply in the wet season following heavy rainfall when the organism is brought to the surface and aerosolised. The dominant risk factors are diabetes, hazardous alcohol use, chronic kidney disease, chronic lung disease and immunosuppression, and the majority of cases occur in people with at least one. Pneumonia is the commonest presentation and may cavitate, and bacteraemic disease seeds abscesses in the spleen, liver, prostate, joints and occasionally the brain, so imaging to search for these collections is part of the standard workup. Treatment has two obligatory phases: an intensive intravenous phase of at least two weeks with meropenem or ceftazidime, extended considerably for deep seated disease, followed by an eradication phase of at least three months with oral trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole. Omitting or shortening the eradication phase is the principal cause of relapse, and the organism is intrinsically resistant to penicillins, first and second generation cephalosporins, aminoglycosides and macrolides.
key_points: Wet season soil and water exposure in northern Australia with diabetes is the classical setting
Cavitating pneumonia with splenic or hepatic abscesses is highly suggestive
The organism is intrinsically resistant to aminoglycosides and to penicillin
Meropenem is preferred over ceftazidime in severe disease with shock
A three month oral eradication phase is mandatory to prevent relapse
explanation.pearls: Always image the prostate in men with melioidosis, since prostatic abscess is common, frequently asymptomatic, and is a recognised source of relapse when it is not drained alongside the antibiotic course.

subtopic_detail: preventing circulatory dysfunction when a large volume of ascitic fluid is drained in one sitting
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 58 year old woman with alcohol related cirrhosis who has been admitted with abdominal distension. She stopped drinking a year ago. She is breathless lying flat, cannot eat more than a few mouthfuls before feeling full, and has gained 9 kg over six weeks.

She already takes spironolactone 400 mg and furosemide 160 mg daily, the maximum tolerated doses, and has been adherent on a 5 g sodium diet. Her abdomen is tensely distended with obvious shifting dullness and her umbilicus is everted. Pulse rate 92 per minute, blood pressure 102/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 per minute, SpO2 95 per cent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius. A diagnostic tap shows 90 neutrophils per microlitre with a serum ascites albumin gradient of 16 g/L. Creatinine is 104 micromol/L (45 to 90), sodium 131 mmol/L (135 to 145), albumin 26 g/L (35 to 50) and international normalised ratio 1.4.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 92 per minute, blood pressure 102/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 per minute, SpO2 95 per cent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Tensely distended abdomen with shifting dullness and everted umbilicus; orthopnoea; no encephalopathy or asterixis; no abdominal tenderness
data_table.Investigations: Ascitic neutrophil count 90 per microlitre with serum ascites albumin gradient 16 g/L; creatinine 104 micromol/L (45 to 90); sodium 131 mmol/L (135 to 145); albumin 26 g/L (35 to 50); international normalised ratio 1.4

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Increase the diuretic doses further and restrict her dietary sodium more strictly, reviewing her weight and electrolytes daily
options.rationale: She is already at the maximum recommended doses of both agents and is adherent to sodium restriction, which defines diuretic resistance rather than undertreatment. Pushing further risks hyponatraemia, acute kidney injury and encephalopathy without relieving the tense ascites. (Source: GESA: Management of ascites in cirrhosis)
source_refs: GESA: Management of ascites in cirrhosis

options.text: Correct her coagulation with fresh frozen plasma before any drainage, given the raised international normalised ratio and low platelets
options.rationale: The prolonged international normalised ratio in cirrhosis reflects reduced synthesis of both procoagulant and anticoagulant factors and does not predict bleeding at paracentesis, which is very low risk. Plasma transfusion adds volume and transfusion risk without measurable benefit. (Source: GESA: Management of ascites in cirrhosis)
source_refs: GESA: Management of ascites in cirrhosis

options.text: Commence intravenous ceftriaxone with albumin on days one and three, treating the ascitic fluid as infected pending culture
options.rationale: Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis requires an ascitic neutrophil count of 250 cells per microlitre or more, and hers is 90 with no fever or abdominal tenderness. Treating an uninfected fluid exposes her to unnecessary antibiotic pressure and does not relieve the distension. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal)

options.text: Perform a large volume paracentesis to dryness and infuse intravenous albumin at about 8 g for every litre of fluid removed
options.rationale: Ascites that persists on maximal tolerated diuretics with dietary adherence is diuretic resistant, and therapeutic paracentesis relieves the symptoms faster and more safely than further diuretic escalation. Albumin replacement of roughly 6 to 8 g per litre removed prevents post-paracentesis circulatory dysfunction with its attendant renal failure and hyponatraemia whenever more than about 5 L is drained. (Source: GESA: Management of ascites in cirrhosis)
source_refs: GESA: Management of ascites in cirrhosis

options.text: Perform a large volume paracentesis to dryness and replace the fluid with intravenous sodium chloride 0.9 per cent as needed
options.rationale: Crystalloid does not maintain oncotic pressure and the sodium load promotes rapid reaccumulation of the ascites. Trials comparing colloid with saline after large volume drainage show higher rates of circulatory dysfunction and renal impairment with saline. (Source: GESA: Management of ascites in cirrhosis)
source_refs: GESA: Management of ascites in cirrhosis

explanation.summary: Ascites is the commonest decompensating event in cirrhosis and carries a poor prognosis, with roughly half of patients dying within two years of its onset, so its appearance should trigger consideration of liver transplantation assessment as well as symptom control. A serum ascites albumin gradient of 11 g/L or more confirms portal hypertension as the mechanism, and the initial treatment is sodium restriction with spironolactone and furosemide in a 100 to 40 mg ratio, titrated to a weight loss of about 0.5 kg daily in the absence of peripheral oedema. Diuretic resistant ascites is defined by a failure to respond despite maximal tolerated doses with genuine dietary adherence, and therapeutic large volume paracentesis is then the treatment of choice. Removing more than about 5 L without colloid replacement precipitates post-paracentesis circulatory dysfunction, a state of accentuated arterial vasodilatation with activation of the renin-angiotensin system that leads to renal impairment, hyponatraemia and shortened survival, and albumin at 6 to 8 g per litre removed prevents it. Coagulopathy as reflected in the international normalised ratio does not contraindicate paracentesis, and options beyond repeated drainage include transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt in selected patients and referral for transplantation.
key_points: A serum ascites albumin gradient of 11 g/L or more confirms portal hypertension
Diuretic resistance is defined by failure at maximal doses with genuine dietary adherence
Albumin 6 to 8 g per litre removed is required when more than about 5 L is drained
The prolonged international normalised ratio in cirrhosis does not predict bleeding at paracentesis
A neutrophil count of 250 per microlitre or more is required to diagnose peritoneal infection
explanation.pearls: Every new presentation of ascites, and every admission of a patient with known ascites, warrants a diagnostic tap with a neutrophil count, because spontaneous bacterial peritonitis is asymptomatic in a substantial minority and is missed entirely if the tap is only performed when the abdomen is tender.

subtopic_detail: screening before immunosuppression in a patient from a region endemic for a persistent helminth
stem:
You are the doctor in a rheumatology clinic planning treatment for a 58 year old woman with newly diagnosed giant cell arteritis. She is about to start prednisolone 50 mg daily with a plan to add tocilizumab.

She was born in a remote community in the Top End and lived there until she was 30, often walking barefoot. She has lived in Melbourne for 28 years and has not returned. She is well apart from the arteritis, has no gastrointestinal symptoms and no cough. Her full blood count shows an eosinophil count of 0.9 x10^9/L (0.0 to 0.5), with the rest of the count, renal function and liver function within normal limits. Hepatitis B and C serology and an interferon gamma release assay for tuberculosis are all negative, and her chest radiograph is normal.

data_table.Examination: No rash, no abdominal tenderness, no respiratory signs; temporal arteries thickened and tender
data_table.Investigations: Eosinophil count 0.9 x10^9/L (0.0 to 0.5) with remainder of full blood count within normal limits; renal and liver function within normal limits; hepatitis B and C serology negative; interferon gamma release assay negative; chest radiograph normal

lead_in: What additional step should be taken before starting immunosuppression?

options.text: Send Strongyloides serology and treat with ivermectin if it is positive, or treat presumptively if the result will be delayed
options.rationale: Strongyloides stercoralis persists for decades through autoinfection and corticosteroids specifically accelerate that cycle, precipitating hyperinfection and disseminated disease with a mortality that can exceed half of those affected. Eosinophilia with prolonged residence in an endemic area of northern Australia makes screening mandatory, and treatment should not wait when high dose corticosteroid is starting imminently. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Send three stool specimens for ova, cysts and parasites and proceed with immunosuppression if all three are negative
options.rationale: Stool microscopy has poor sensitivity for Strongyloides because larval output is low and intermittent, and even serial specimens miss a substantial proportion of infections. Relying on negative stool microscopy provides false reassurance before immunosuppression. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Repeat the eosinophil count in four weeks and investigate for a parasitic cause only if the eosinophilia persists or rises
options.rationale: Corticosteroids suppress the eosinophil count within hours, so repeating it after starting prednisolone destroys its diagnostic value. Delaying investigation also leaves the window in which hyperinfection develops unmonitored. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Commence prophylactic trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for the duration of her corticosteroid therapy and proceed as planned
options.rationale: Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole prophylaxis is indicated against Pneumocystis jirovecii during prolonged high dose corticosteroid therapy and should be considered separately here. It does not treat Strongyloides, for which ivermectin is required. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Arrange a bone marrow biopsy and peripheral blood flow cytometry to investigate the unexplained eosinophilia before treatment
options.rationale: Haematological investigation of eosinophilia is appropriate when the count is markedly raised without an identified cause, particularly above 1.5 x10^9/L with organ damage. A modest eosinophilia with a clear epidemiological exposure should first prompt parasitic screening. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Strongyloidiasis)

explanation.summary: Strongyloides stercoralis is unique among human helminths in completing its entire life cycle within the host through autoinfection, so untreated infection persists for decades after a person leaves an endemic area, and in Australia it is endemic in parts of northern Australia as well as being common in migrants from Southeast Asia, the Pacific and sub-Saharan Africa. Chronic infection is usually asymptomatic or produces intermittent abdominal symptoms, an urticarial rash and a mild eosinophilia, which is frequently the only clue. Corticosteroids directly accelerate the autoinfective cycle through effects on the parasite itself, and hyperinfection syndrome produces massive larval migration with pneumonitis, ileus and Gram negative bacteraemia or meningitis from enteric organisms carried across the bowel wall, with a very high mortality. Serology is the screening test of choice since stool microscopy is insensitive, and treatment is ivermectin, usually as two doses two weeks apart with serological follow up to confirm cure. Screening before commencing corticosteroids or other immunosuppression in anyone with relevant residential or travel history is the standard of care, and when treatment cannot wait for the serology, presumptive ivermectin is given.
key_points: Autoinfection allows infection to persist for decades after leaving an endemic area
Eosinophilia may be the only sign of chronic infection and is suppressed by corticosteroids
Serology, not stool microscopy, is the screening test of choice
Corticosteroids directly precipitate hyperinfection with very high mortality
Ivermectin is the treatment; presumptive therapy is given when immunosuppression cannot wait
explanation.pearls: Recurrent Gram negative bacteraemia or Escherichia coli meningitis in an immunosuppressed patient from an endemic region should raise strongyloides hyperinfection, because migrating larvae carry enteric organisms across the bowel wall and the parasitic diagnosis is otherwise easily missed.

subtopic_detail: separating volume overload from an immune reaction when dyspnoea follows a red cell transfusion
stem:
You are the doctor on a medical ward called to a 79 year old woman who has become breathless. She is receiving her second unit of red cells for iron deficiency anaemia from chronic gastrointestinal blood loss, and the unit is 40 minutes in. She has a history of chronic heart failure with a reduced ejection fraction and takes furosemide, which was withheld this morning.

Pulse rate 104 per minute, blood pressure 168/94 mmHg, respiratory rate 30 per minute, SpO2 88 per cent on room air, temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius. The jugular venous pressure is elevated at 6 cm above the sternal angle, there are bilateral basal crackles and new pitting oedema to the mid shins. There is no rash, no urticaria, no wheeze and no back or loin pain. Chest radiograph shows bilateral perihilar interstitial infiltrates with upper lobe venous diversion and small pleural effusions, and the cardiothoracic ratio is increased compared with a film from last year.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 104 per minute, blood pressure 168/94 mmHg, respiratory rate 30 per minute, SpO2 88 per cent on room air, temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Jugular venous pressure elevated 6 cm above the sternal angle; bilateral basal crackles; new pitting oedema to mid shins; no rash, urticaria or wheeze
data_table.Investigations: Chest radiograph shows bilateral perihilar interstitial infiltrates, upper lobe venous diversion, small bilateral pleural effusions and an increased cardiothoracic ratio compared with a prior film

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Stop the transfusion, send the unit and a clotted sample for a haemolysis workup, and commence intravenous fluid to protect renal function
options.rationale: Acute haemolytic reaction from ABO incompatibility presents with fever, rigors, loin pain and dark urine, and this workup should be triggered by those features. Fluid loading a woman with pulmonary oedema on the basis of an unsupported suspicion would be harmful. (Source: Australian Red Cross Lifeblood: Transfusion reactions)
source_refs: Australian Red Cross Lifeblood: Transfusion reactions

options.text: Slow the transfusion rate, give oral paracetamol and an antihistamine, and complete the remainder of the unit under closer observation
options.rationale: Premedication and a slower rate are the response to a mild febrile non-haemolytic or allergic reaction, and continuing the unit in established pulmonary oedema adds further volume. She has no fever and no allergic features. (Source: Australian Red Cross Lifeblood: Transfusion reactions)
source_refs: Australian Red Cross Lifeblood: Transfusion reactions

options.text: Stop the transfusion, sit her upright with oxygen, and give an intravenous loop diuretic with close monitoring of her response
options.rationale: Hypertension with a raised jugular venous pressure, new peripheral oedema and radiographic upper lobe venous diversion identify circulatory overload rather than an immune reaction, and diuresis with upright posture and oxygen reverses it. Stopping the transfusion halts further volume loading while the assessment continues. (Source: Australian Red Cross Lifeblood: Transfusion reactions)
source_refs: Australian Red Cross Lifeblood: Transfusion reactions

options.text: Stop the transfusion, give supportive oxygen and consider ventilatory support, and avoid diuretics as the intravascular volume is not raised
options.rationale: This describes the management of transfusion related acute lung injury, which is the near pair to this presentation but characteristically produces hypotension, fever and a normal or low jugular venous pressure with no cardiomegaly. Withholding diuretics in genuine circulatory overload would prolong the hypoxaemia. (Source: Australian Red Cross Lifeblood: Transfusion reactions)
source_refs: Australian Red Cross Lifeblood: Transfusion reactions

options.text: Stop the transfusion, give intramuscular adrenaline and intravenous fluid, and commence a continuous adrenaline infusion if required
options.rationale: Anaphylaxis to a blood component causes urticaria, angio-oedema, wheeze and hypotension within minutes, and none of those features are present. Giving fluid to a patient in pulmonary oedema would worsen her condition considerably. (Source: ASCIA: Acute management of anaphylaxis)

explanation.summary: Transfusion associated circulatory overload is among the most frequently reported causes of transfusion related morbidity and death, and is systematically underdiagnosed because it is mistaken for other acute reactions. It arises when the transfused volume exceeds what the circulation can accommodate, and the risk is concentrated in older patients, those with heart failure or renal impairment, small body size, and those receiving multiple units or concurrent intravenous fluids. The features that distinguish it are hypertension, a raised jugular venous pressure, a third heart sound, peripheral oedema, cardiomegaly and radiographic upper lobe venous diversion, alongside a rapid response to diuresis. Transfusion related acute lung injury is the principal differential and typically produces hypotension with fever, a normal jugular venous pressure and bilateral infiltrates without cardiomegaly, and it is managed with respiratory support rather than diuretics. Prevention in at risk patients includes transfusing one unit at a time with reassessment, using a slower infusion rate, and giving a diuretic between units where clinically appropriate.
key_points: Hypertension with a raised jugular venous pressure and oedema indicates circulatory overload
Transfusion related acute lung injury produces hypotension with a normal jugular venous pressure
Upper lobe venous diversion and cardiomegaly support the overload diagnosis
Rapid improvement with diuresis is both treatment and confirmation
Prevent by transfusing single units with reassessment in at risk patients
explanation.pearls: Prescribe one unit at a time with clinical reassessment before the next in any patient over 70 or with heart failure or renal impairment, since single unit transfusion policy is the most effective single measure for preventing transfusion associated circulatory overload.

subtopic_detail: confirming reversibility before referring a gait and continence syndrome for a shunt
stem:
You are the geriatric medicine registrar assessing a 76 year old man referred with fourteen months of progressive walking difficulty. His wife says his feet seem stuck to the floor when he starts to walk and when he turns, though he walks better holding a trolley. He has had urinary urgency for six months with three episodes of incontinence. She also reports that he is slower to answer questions and has lost interest in the newspaper.

He has no resting tremor and his arm swing is preserved. His steps are short with a wide base and outwardly rotated feet, and he takes six steps to turn. He scores 24 out of 30 on a cognitive screen with the losses in attention and executive items and preserved recall. A three month trial of levodopa at adequate dose produced no change. Magnetic resonance imaging shows ventriculomegaly with an Evans index of 0.37, a callosal angle of 62 degrees, and tight high convexity sulci with enlarged sylvian fissures. There is mild small vessel change but no infarct.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits with no postural drop
data_table.Examination: Magnetic gait with short wide based steps, outward foot rotation and a six step turn; preserved arm swing; no resting tremor; no cogwheel rigidity; cognitive screen 24 out of 30 with attentional and executive losses and preserved recall
data_table.Investigations: Magnetic resonance imaging shows Evans index 0.37, callosal angle 62 degrees, tight high convexity sulci with enlarged sylvian fissures, mild small vessel change and no infarct; no response to a three month trial of levodopa

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer him directly for ventriculoperitoneal shunt insertion on the basis of the clinical triad and the supporting imaging findings
options.rationale: Ventriculomegaly is common in older adults and much of it reflects atrophy rather than hydrocephalus, so shunting on imaging and symptoms alone exposes patients with irreversible disease to a procedure carrying real rates of subdural haematoma, infection and shunt failure. Predictive testing precedes surgery. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Normal pressure hydrocephalus)
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Normal pressure hydrocephalus

options.text: Increase the levodopa dose substantially and reassess his gait after a further eight weeks of higher dose therapy
options.rationale: Absent response to an adequate levodopa trial is itself a discriminating finding that argues against idiopathic Parkinson disease, and the preserved arm swing and absent tremor point the same way. Escalating a drug that has already failed adds adverse effects without diagnostic value. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Attribute the syndrome to cerebral small vessel disease, optimise vascular risk factors and refer for gait rehabilitation
options.rationale: Vascular parkinsonism is the closest differential and can produce an almost identical lower body gait disorder, but it usually follows a stepwise course with extensive white matter disease and often pyramidal signs, whereas his imaging shows only mild change with a narrow callosal angle. Vascular risk management should still occur but would leave a potentially reversible condition untreated. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Normal pressure hydrocephalus)
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Normal pressure hydrocephalus

options.text: Commence a cholinesterase inhibitor for probable Alzheimer disease and arrange formal neuropsychological assessment in six months
options.rationale: Alzheimer disease produces an amnestic profile with impaired recall that does not improve with cueing, and gait disturbance appears late rather than leading the presentation. His preserved recall with attentional and executive losses indicates a subcortical pattern. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Normal pressure hydrocephalus)
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Normal pressure hydrocephalus

options.text: Perform a high volume lumbar puncture with quantified gait timing before and after, and refer to neurosurgery if he improves
options.rationale: A magnetic gait with urinary urgency and a subcortical cognitive pattern, with imaging showing a narrow callosal angle and tight high convexity sulci and no levodopa response, fits normal pressure hydrocephalus, but imaging alone predicts shunt response poorly. Removing 30 to 50 mL of cerebrospinal fluid with objective gait measurement before and after is the accepted test of reversibility and selects those who will benefit from surgery. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: Normal pressure hydrocephalus)
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice: Normal pressure hydrocephalus

explanation.summary: Normal pressure hydrocephalus is characterised by a gait disorder, urinary urgency or incontinence and a subcortical cognitive impairment in the setting of communicating ventricular enlargement with a normal opening pressure, and its importance lies in being one of the few potentially reversible causes of dementia and gait failure in older adults. The gait is the earliest and most shunt responsive feature, described as magnetic or glue footed, with short wide based steps, reduced foot clearance, outward foot rotation and marked difficulty turning, while arm swing is typically preserved. Imaging findings that support the diagnosis beyond simple ventriculomegaly include an Evans index above 0.3, a callosal angle below about 90 degrees, and disproportionately enlarged subarachnoid space hydrocephalus with tight high convexity sulci alongside widened sylvian fissures. Because ventriculomegaly from atrophy is common and shunting carries meaningful surgical risk, prediction of response matters, and a high volume lumbar puncture removing 30 to 50 mL of cerebrospinal fluid with objective timed gait measurement before and after, or extended external lumbar drainage in equivocal cases, is used to select surgical candidates. A positive test predicts benefit well, whereas a negative test does not entirely exclude response and may warrant extended drainage.
key_points: Gait is the earliest feature and the one most likely to respond to shunting
The cognitive profile is subcortical with preserved recall, unlike Alzheimer disease
A narrow callosal angle and tight high convexity sulci support the diagnosis
Ventriculomegaly alone predicts shunt response poorly and often reflects atrophy
High volume lumbar puncture with objective gait timing is the selection test
explanation.pearls: Measure the gait objectively with a timed up and go or a ten metre walk immediately before and two to four hours after the tap, since subjective impressions from the patient and family are unreliable and a measured improvement of more than about ten per cent is what predicts shunt benefit.
