subtopic_detail: sequencing cooling and transfer in exertional hyperthermia with central nervous system dysfunction
stem:
You are the doctor at a medical tent at a summer fun run when a 24 year old man collapses 400 m from the finish. The ambient temperature is 36 degrees Celsius with high humidity. He is confused, combative and does not know where he is. Bystanders say he was running normally until he staggered and fell.

He is not a known epileptic, takes no regular medication and has taken no recreational drugs according to his running partner. Pulse rate 148 per minute, blood pressure 96/52 mmHg, respiratory rate 32 per minute, SpO2 97 per cent on room air, rectal temperature 41.6 degrees Celsius. His skin is hot and sweaty. Capillary glucose is 5.8 mmol/L. There is no neck stiffness, no rash and no head injury. The tent has ice, several large tubs of water, intravenous fluids and a monitor. The nearest emergency department is fifteen minutes away by road and an ambulance has been called.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 148 per minute, blood pressure 96/52 mmHg, respiratory rate 32 per minute, SpO2 97 per cent on room air, rectal temperature 41.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Confused and combative with no orientation to place; skin hot and sweaty; no neck stiffness, rash or evidence of head injury; capillary glucose 5.8 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.text: Give intravenous midazolam to control the agitation and reassess his temperature once he is settled and safe to handle
options.rationale: Benzodiazepines have a role in controlling shivering and severe agitation that obstructs cooling, but they are an adjunct rather than the priority. Sedating first and reassessing later delays the intervention that determines survival. (Source: ANZCOR: Heat induced illness)

options.text: Begin cold water immersion on site immediately and continue until the core temperature falls to about 39 degrees Celsius
options.rationale: Exertional heat stroke outcome is determined by the time spent above a core temperature of roughly 40 degrees Celsius, so cooling must begin where the patient is rather than after transport, and cold water immersion achieves the fastest cooling rate of any available method. Stopping at about 39 degrees Celsius avoids overshoot into hypothermia. (Source: ANZCOR: Heat induced illness)

options.text: Transfer him urgently by ambulance with the air conditioning on maximum and commence active cooling on arrival at hospital
options.rationale: Transport before cooling is the single most consequential error in exertional heat stroke, since every additional minute above 40 degrees Celsius increases the risk of multiorgan failure and death. The rule is to cool first and transport second. (Source: ANZCOR: Heat induced illness)

options.text: Give intravenous paracetamol and cold intravenous fluid, then apply ice packs to the groin, axillae and neck while awaiting transport
options.rationale: Antipyretics act on a hypothalamic set point that is not raised in heat stroke and are ineffective while adding hepatotoxic risk in a patient who may develop liver injury. Ice packs and cold fluids cool far more slowly than immersion and are fallbacks when immersion is impossible. (Source: ANZCOR: Heat induced illness)

options.text: Give intravenous dantrolene and commence aggressive crystalloid resuscitation while arranging urgent transfer to intensive care
options.rationale: Dantrolene treats malignant hyperthermia, in which a triggering anaesthetic agent produces muscle rigidity and hypercarbia, and trials have shown no benefit in exertional heat stroke. Fluid is needed but does not substitute for physical cooling. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

explanation.summary: Exertional heat stroke is defined by a core temperature above 40 degrees Celsius with central nervous system dysfunction in the context of physical exertion, and it is distinguished from heat exhaustion precisely by that neurological involvement, which may be confusion, combativeness, ataxia, seizure or coma. Sweating is often preserved in the exertional form, so dry skin should never be required to make the diagnosis, and temperature must be measured rectally because oral, tympanic and axillary readings substantially underestimate the core in this setting. Survival correlates with the duration of time spent above a core temperature of about 40 degrees Celsius, which makes immediate on site cooling the single most important intervention and places it before transport in every recommended protocol. Cold water immersion produces the fastest cooling rates and is the method of choice where a tub is available, with cooling stopped at around 38.5 to 39 degrees Celsius to avoid overshoot. Complications include rhabdomyolysis, acute kidney injury, disseminated intravascular coagulation, hepatic failure and acute respiratory distress syndrome, all of which are less frequent when cooling has been rapid.
key_points: Core temperature above 40 degrees Celsius with neurological dysfunction defines heat stroke
Sweating is often preserved in the exertional form and does not exclude it
Rectal temperature is required; peripheral sites underestimate the core substantially
Cool first and transport second; time above 40 degrees Celsius determines outcome
Antipyretics and dantrolene are ineffective in this condition
explanation.pearls: Cold water immersion achieves cooling rates of roughly 0.2 degrees Celsius per minute compared with about 0.05 for ice packs and evaporative methods, which is why a tub of iced water at an endurance event is a life saving piece of equipment rather than an optional comfort measure.

subtopic_detail: modifying the resuscitation algorithm when cardiac arrest occurs at a very low core temperature
stem:
You are the doctor receiving a 46 year old bushwalker retrieved from an alpine area after a night lost in sleet. He was found unresponsive. On arrival he is in cardiac arrest with ventricular fibrillation on the monitor, and cardiopulmonary resuscitation is in progress.

His oesophageal temperature reads 27.4 degrees Celsius. He has been shocked once at the scene without response and has received no drugs. He is intubated with good chest rise and end tidal carbon dioxide of 14 mmHg. His clothing has been cut away and he is being dried. Potassium is 4.1 mmol/L (3.5 to 5.5), glucose 6.2 mmol/L and lactate 7 mmol/L (less than 2.0). The hospital has cardiothoracic surgery with extracorporeal membrane oxygenation capability on site and the perfusion team has been alerted.

data_table.Vital signs: Cardiac arrest with ventricular fibrillation; oesophageal temperature 27.4 degrees Celsius; end tidal carbon dioxide 14 mmHg during compressions
data_table.Examination: Unresponsive, intubated with good bilateral chest rise; clothing removed and patient being dried; no evidence of major trauma
data_table.Investigations: Potassium 4.1 mmol/L (3.5 to 5.5); glucose 6.2 mmol/L; lactate 7 mmol/L (less than 2.0)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Continue compressions while rewarming with warmed intravenous fluid and forced air blankets, and cease efforts if there is no response in thirty minutes
options.rationale: External and minimally invasive rewarming achieves only around 1 to 2 degrees Celsius per hour, which is far too slow for a patient in arrest, and a fixed thirty minute limit ignores the neuroprotection that profound hypothermia confers. Prolonged resuscitation with full recovery is well documented in this group. (Source: ANZCOR: Hypothermia)

options.text: Cease resuscitation, since an end tidal carbon dioxide of 14 mmHg and a lactate of 7 mmol/L indicate futility in a prolonged arrest
options.rationale: The usual prognostic markers are unreliable in profound hypothermia because metabolic rate and carbon dioxide production are markedly reduced, so a low end tidal value reflects the temperature rather than the quality of resuscitation. A normal potassium here is the finding that argues strongly against futility. (Source: ANZCOR: Hypothermia)

options.text: Give intravenous amiodarone 300 mg and magnesium sulfate 10 mmol, then repeat defibrillation at two minute intervals
options.rationale: Antiarrhythmic drugs are ineffective in the hypothermic myocardium and accumulate because hepatic metabolism and renal clearance are profoundly slowed. Their delayed effects can provoke arrhythmia during the rewarming phase. (Source: ANZCOR: Hypothermia)

options.text: Continue compressions, withhold further shocks and adrenaline for now, and transfer him for extracorporeal rewarming
options.rationale: Below about 30 degrees Celsius the myocardium responds poorly to defibrillation and drugs accumulate without effect while toxicity builds on rewarming, so further shocks and adrenaline are withheld until the core temperature rises. A potassium of 4.1 mmol/L indicates the hypothermia preceded rather than followed the arrest, and extracorporeal rewarming offers the best survival with intact neurology in this situation. (Source: ANZCOR: Hypothermia)

options.text: Deliver repeated stacked shocks at maximum energy and give adrenaline 1 mg every three to five minutes as per the standard algorithm
options.rationale: The standard algorithm assumes a normothermic myocardium, and at 27 degrees Celsius repeated shocks are usually ineffective while repeated adrenaline doses accumulate and can cause toxicity and arrhythmia once the patient is rewarmed. Modification of the algorithm is specifically recommended below 30 degrees Celsius. (Source: ANZCOR: Hypothermia)

explanation.summary: Accidental hypothermia with cardiac arrest is one of the few situations in which standard advanced life support is deliberately modified, because the profoundly cooled myocardium is refractory to both defibrillation and drugs while cerebral metabolic demand is so reduced that neurologically intact survival after very prolonged resuscitation is well documented. Below about 30 degrees Celsius, current guidance is to limit defibrillation attempts and withhold adrenaline and antiarrhythmics until the core temperature rises, then to give drugs at extended intervals between 30 and 35 degrees Celsius. Extracorporeal life support provides rewarming rates far beyond any other method and carries the best survival with good neurological outcome, so transfer to a centre with that capability should be arranged early rather than after other measures have failed. Prognostication is deliberately conservative, and the serum potassium is the most useful discriminator, since a markedly raised level indicates cell lysis and suggests the patient was asphyxiated or died before cooling, whereas a normal potassium supports continued resuscitation. Handling must also be gentle, because rough movement of a profoundly cold heart can itself precipitate ventricular fibrillation.
key_points: Below 30 degrees Celsius, limit shocks and withhold adrenaline until rewarming begins
Give drugs at extended intervals between 30 and 35 degrees Celsius
Extracorporeal rewarming gives the best survival with intact neurology
A markedly raised potassium suggests the arrest preceded the cooling
Standard prognostic markers including end tidal carbon dioxide are unreliable when cold
explanation.pearls: Nobody is dead until they are warm and dead, and the practical exception is a serum potassium above roughly 12 mmol/L in an avalanche or immersion victim, which indicates hypoxic death before cooling and is the accepted biochemical marker for stopping resuscitation.
